title: VAR-Q: Tuning-free KV Cache Quantization for Visual Autoregressive Image and Video Generation
text: Title: VAR-Q: Tuning-free KV Cache Quantization for Visual Autoregressive Image and Video Generation Boxun Xu , Jiaji Lu , Yuxuan Yin , Zihu Wang , Ziyue Liu , Yu Wang , Zirui Liu , Peng Li Comments: A preliminary version of this work was presented at the ICCV 2025 BiVision Workshop Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Performance (cs.PF) Visual autoregressive generation spans two dominant paradigms: next-scale prediction for images and video, and next-frame prediction for video. Both decode block-by-block rather than token-by-token, yielding KV caches whose statistics diverge from those of language models. At scale, KV memory exceeds the weights and limits large-scale deployment caused by a large amount of visual tokens. Our analysis of these caches reveals three findings. First, a small set of massive-value channels carries the functional load: ablating these outlier channels collapses generation, whereas ablating a matched set of inlier channels leaves quality intact. Second, the outliers organize along two axes, feature and block, with magnitudes persistent within each cell and shifting across cells. Third, this structure arises from two independent mechanisms: projection bias and RoPE-induced scattering. Guided by these findings, we propose VAR-Q, a tuning-free KV-cache quantization framework that groups along the same two axes. The generation loop provides block boundaries for free, removing the need for outlier detection or calibration. Paired with bit-packing kernels for runtime memory reduction, VAR-Q delivers low-bit quantization across nine models spanning both paradigms, cutting KV memory by up to 78.5% with negligible quality degradation and enabling 6x larger inference batches.

title: Discourse Analysis of Legislative Bill Discussions
text: Title: Discourse Analysis of Legislative Bill Discussions Isaac Rudnick , Nipun Das , Foaad Khosmood Comments: 10 pages, 4 figures Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) Legislative hearings are distinct communication events with their own human recognizable structure and logic, yet they have been analyzed as distinct phenomena beyond their transcripts. Understanding legislative hearings at a deeper level is a major step in analyzing the work and power relationships within democratic bodies. In this work, we present a novel end-to-end pipeline for parsing rhetorical structures from legislative committee hearings with the goal of improving legislative discourse analysis and democratic accountability. We also propose a rhetorical structure grammar and find that 55.21% of California state bill discussions in our dataset can be parsed with this grammar. We evaluate our pipeline with two utterance section classifiers on a random subset of over 2,000 annotated utterances corresponding to 100 hearings. We find that a logistic regression-based classifier with grammar-based output masking and utterance tag smoothing outperforms more complex models, achieving an F1 score of 52.8% against our ground truth discourse section labels.

title: DS@GT ARC at CheckThat! 2026: A Verdict-Anchored Pipeline for Generating Fact-Checking Articles
text: Title: DS@GT ARC at CheckThat! 2026: A Verdict-Anchored Pipeline for Generating Fact-Checking Articles Hoang Thanh Thanh Truong , Shuyu Tian Comments: CLEF 2026 Working Notes, 21 - 24 September 2026, Jena, Germany Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) Misinformation spreads faster than professional fact-checkers can manually verify it and write articles explaining their verdicts. This creates a need to automate the production of fact-checking articles. This paper details work done by the DS@GT ARC team for CLEF 2026 CheckThat! Lab Task 3 Fact-Checking Article Generation. We seek to generate a full fact-checking article from a claim, its original verdict, and a set of scraped source documents. Our team built a four-stage pipeline that cleans noisy evidence, retrieves and clusters relevant sources, generates the article by conditioning \texttt{Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct} on the original fact-checker verdict, and recovers inline citations through deterministic post-processing. We achieved a mean score of 0.428 and ranked 3rd out of 9 teams for the CLEF 2026 CheckThat! Lab Task 3, compared to a baseline mean score of 0.272. Our code is available on GitHub at this https URL .

title: CCDWIKI: Decoupling Case Formulation from Response Generation in Longitudinal CBT Dialogue
text: Title: CCDWIKI: Decoupling Case Formulation from Response Generation in Longitudinal CBT Dialogue Mingwen Zhang , Ruiyang Song , Qinying Wang , Yuchen Wang , Changsheng Ma , Minqiang Yang Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) demands more than empathic validation, requiring instead a structured formulation of the interplay among situations, automatic thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. Therapists formalize this interplay through a Cognitive Conceptualization Diagram, where maintaining longitudinal coherence necessitates continuous evidential adjudication to separate tentative hypotheses from established findings. Current dialogue systems track conversational history via retrieval or static profiles but lack the representational capacity to encode epistemic status. Consequently, provisional interpretations are often prematurely reified as established facts, inadvertently biasing downstream interventions. Addressing this limitation, CCDWiki is introduced as a plug-and-play advisor conceptualizing longitudinal therapy as evidence-grounded hypothesis adjudication. The approach encodes each clinical hypothesis as a mutable entry bound to corroborating and contradicting evidence. Across sessions, accumulating data strengthens supported entries, preserves provisional ones, and retracts contradicted assumptions. The resulting formulation distills into concise guidance for unmodified therapeutic language models. Experiments demonstrate substantial improvements in both conceptualization and intervention quality without requiring backbone retraining.

title: Human-like cross-language generalisation in deep neural speaker embeddings and its acoustic foundations
text: Title: Human-like cross-language generalisation in deep neural speaker embeddings and its acoustic foundations Tianze Xu , Xiyang Li , Xiaoming Jiang , Volker Dellwo Comments: This manuscript has been accepted for presentation at Interspeech 2026. Code is available at this https URL . The archived release is available on Zenodo at this https URL Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) ; Sound (cs.SD); Audio and Speech Processing (eess.AS) Generalisability is a central question for deep neural networks, including the cross-language generalisation of speaker embeddings. This study examined whether deep neural speaker embeddings generalise across languages and how such generalisation relates to human perception and acoustic structure. Using Cantonese--English bilingual speech presented in within- and cross-language conditions, we derived similarity from 18 state-of-the-art models and compared it with human ratings and acoustic features using linear mixed models and representational similarity analysis. Embeddings exhibited cross-language generalisation that broadly paralleled human behaviour, reflecting accurate identity discrimination and sensitivity to language switching. This generalisation relied on largely shared acoustic cues with language-sensitive weighting, mirroring human patterns. Together, these findings provide converging evidence for human--machine alignment in cross-language voice similarity processing.

title: Same Origin, Different Verdicts: Text Production Conditions Confound Machine-Generated Text Detection in Russian
text: Title: Same Origin, Different Verdicts: Text Production Conditions Confound Machine-Generated Text Detection in Russian Stanislav Kirichenko Comments: 65 pages, 6 figures, 24 tables. English translation of the frozen Russian manuscript; the Russian text is the source of record and is available with all data, code and run manifests at this https URL (v1.0.1) Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) Automated detection of machine-generated text is applied where the verdict carries a cost for the author, yet origin is a property of the production process, not an observable property of the text. The conditions under which a text is produced push it in the same direction in which a generative model is presumed to push it. This study measures the contribution of these conditions while origin is held fixed. The Russian-language corpus of 1882 documents comprises a machine part, generated by four generation channels (each backed by its own model family) across 45 tasks in three task modes, and an archival human part annotated for source regimentation level before the texts were read. The primary contrast is computed within the machine corpus: both halves of a pair are generated by the same model for the same task and differ only in task wording. Machine-likeness is measured by four operationalisations: an interpretable index with weights fixed before data collection, a trained classifier, a zero-shot metric on an open model, a judge model. The main result is disagreement between procedures: changing the task mode shifted the scores of all four, but three gave a negative shift, the judge a positive one, and none of the four intervals covers zero. The comparison plan and the specifications of procedures 2-4 were fixed after the result of procedure 1, before procedures 2-4 ran; the disagreement survived correction of a corpus defect and of the nested validation. A baseline on the source identifier alone reaches a median AUROC of 1.0000 on the thirteen group splits where it is defined, and removing emphasis markers flipped a confident machine verdict to human without changing the full text by a single character. The scores are properties of a specific measurement system and corpus: they reflect data collection, repetition, formatting, and preprocessing decisions as well as linguistic style.

title: SRRM: A Retrieval-Reconstruction Benchmark for Evaluating Long-Context Memory in Small Language Models
text: Title: SRRM: A Retrieval-Reconstruction Benchmark for Evaluating Long-Context Memory in Small Language Models Christopher Alberto Hamonangan Comments: 37 pages, 20 tables, 13 figures Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) Small Language Models (SLMs) are increasingly deployed on consumer-grade hardware, yet their ability to preserve information across progressively longer contexts remains insufficiently understood. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate retrieval-oriented tasks, providing limited insight into whether successful retrieval reflects comprehensive long-context memory preservation. To address this limitation, this paper introduces Simple Retrieval-Reconstruction Memory (SRRM), a lightweight and fully reproducible benchmark that jointly evaluates Targeted Retrieval and Global Information Reconstruction. This study also proposes the Memory Preservation Ratio (MPR), a benchmark-level metric that quantifies the relationship between retrieval and reconstruction performance. SRRM was evaluated using a synthetic dataset on three Qwen2.5 models (0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters) across context loads ranging from 10 to 100 factual statements. Experimental results show that reconstruction performance deteriorated substantially faster than retrieval accuracy as contextual information increased, indicating that retrieval alone is insufficient to characterize long-context memory preservation. Among the evaluated models, Qwen2.5-1.5B achieved the highest retrieval accuracy (86.7%), reconstruction performance (45.7%), and MPR (0.53), outperforming the larger Qwen2.5-3B model (72.2%, 18.5%, and 0.26, respectively). These findings demonstrate that increasing parameter count does not necessarily improve long-context memory preservation. Overall, SRRM provides a reproducible and extensible benchmark for systematically evaluating long-context memory while revealing complementary memory behaviors that remain hidden under retrieval-only evaluation frameworks.

title: Deterministic Network Interface Naming on Multi-NIC Linux Systems: A Boot-Time Convergence Approach
text: Title: Deterministic Network Interface Naming on Multi-NIC Linux Systems: A Boot-Time Convergence Approach Chetan Nigudgi Comments: 10 pages, 2 figures Subjects: Operating Systems (cs.OS) Network interface naming on multi-NIC Linux systems suffers from a well-documented race condition in systemd-udevd that has remained unsolved since 2017. When multiple network interfaces are present, parallel udev worker threads attempt to rename interfaces simultaneously, causing EEXIST failures when a target name is temporarily occupied by another interface awaiting its own rename. The upstream systemd project has classified this as "not-a-bug" and declines to implement a fix. The problem, previously cosmetic under NetworkManager, has become critical as the industry migrates to systemd-networkd, which matches interfaces by name rather than MAC address, turning a failed rename into a complete loss of network connectivity. This paper presents a boot-time convergence approach that combines systemd .link file declarations with a retry-based init service that detects and recovers from rename failures before dependent services start. Deployed across diverse multi-NIC hardware configurations, the solution achieves 100% deterministic interface naming. The approach is OS-agnostic and applicable to any systemd-based Linux distribution.

title: Streaming OS Installation from Compressed Partitioned Images on Memory-Constrained Bare-Metal Hosts
text: Title: Streaming OS Installation from Compressed Partitioned Images on Memory-Constrained Bare-Metal Hosts Chetan Nigudgi , Chip Cary Comments: 7 pages, 2 figures Subjects: Operating Systems (cs.OS) Bare-metal server provisioning systems typically decompress OS images into RAM before writing them to disk. When servers have insufficient RAM to hold the decompressed image (increasingly common as OS images grow due to AI/ML toolkits, GPU drivers, and firmware stacks), provisioning fails entirely. This paper presents a streaming installation technique that combines partial decompression for metadata extraction with pipeline-based disk writing, enabling OS installation on hosts where available RAM is less than the decompressed image size. The method decompresses only the first 30MB of a compressed image to extract the GPT partition table, calculates the target filesystem offset, then streams the full image through a kernel pipe buffer (64KB) directly to disk at the calculated offset, never storing the decompressed data in memory or on disk. Deployed across a production fleet of memory-constrained bare-metal servers, the technique achieves 100% provisioning success where the standard approach fails entirely.

title: AI-Driven SaaS Platform Integration: AI Express for Unified Generative AI Services with Pay-As-You-Go Credit Systems and Scalable Microservice Architecture
text: Title: AI-Driven SaaS Platform Integration: AI Express for Unified Generative AI Services with Pay-As-You-Go Credit Systems and Scalable Microservice Architecture Deepit Sapru Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Software Engineering (cs.SE) Generative AI is currently fragmented, with separate subscriptions required for text generation, image synthesis, and code assistance, leading to high costs and workflow disruptions. AI Express is a SaaS platform that consolidates these capabilities into a unified pay-as-you-go service. The platform provides a range of AI tools, including a Core Code Reviewer that evaluates GitHub repositories, a Text-to-Website generator that converts text into fully functional websites, script generation, grammar checking, data analysis, and watermark removal, all accessible through a single interface without requiring technical expertise.

title: Who May Overrule the Agent? Evidence-Gated Authority in LLM Review Institutions
text: Title: Who May Overrule the Agent? Evidence-Gated Authority in LLM Review Institutions Fuad Ali Comments: 11 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Code, frozen outputs, and reproduction instructions: this https URL Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Multiagent Systems (cs.MA) Multi-agent language-model systems often add a reviewer to improve an upstream agent's decision. Yet a reviewer can both repair errors and replace decisions that were already correct. We study this as a problem of institutional jurisdiction: conditional on the same proposal, task information, model, and review output, when is the reviewer authorized to make its recommendation binding? We compare broad override authority with an evidence gate that permits replacement only after the reviewer produces a mechanically valid record of a binding-constraint violation and a compliant repair. Across two locally run open-weight models, 96 spatial-policy tasks, and a 96-task portfolio-transfer benchmark, the gate sharply reduces corruption of correct proposals while retaining most repairs of violations. The directions of this tradeoff are partly implied by the rule; its magnitude depends on reviewer transitions and upstream proposal states. A prospective validation then gives the reviewer an explicit choice to retain, replace, or escalate. This eliminates correct-proposal corruption for Qwen, but Mistral still replaces all 48 correct proposals; Qwen also declines every welfare-only repair that Mistral frequently attempts. Thus interface design changes reviewer behavior but is not a model-independent safeguard. The result is not that restricted review is universally better. It is that reviewer competence, action interface, and binding jurisdiction jointly determine both the correction domain and the corruption surface.

title: Agent Harness Awareness: Turning Verified Telemetry into Operational Control for Tool-Using Agents
text: Title: Agent Harness Awareness: Turning Verified Telemetry into Operational Control for Tool-Using Agents Manu Agrawal , Shrey Nagpal Comments: 9 pages, 3 figures Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Computation and Language (cs.CL) Tool descriptions tell an agent what an action can do, but they do not necessarily reveal whether that action is healthy or suitable at the moment of use. Execution harnesses often possess this information through monitors, traces, and recent failures while the model choosing the next action does not. We call this gap operational blindness. We introduce Agent Harness Awareness, a trust-separated design in which the host supplies a small, fresh, verified state snapshot before a consequential action while retaining measurement, enforcement, evaluation, and final dispatch authority. We test its tools-and-network instance with ToolRoute, a controlled isolation benchmark that holds the task and candidate semantics constant and varies the operational information available to the model. In a 216-decision ablation across GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Sonnet 5, and Gemini 3.7 Flash, verified tool-health state reduced mean observable policy regret by 96.9% against a same-shape neutral control (4,252 ms to 131 ms) and raised single-dispatch completion from 69.4% to 95.8%. In a separate 27-decision end-to-end replication with live local TCP/HTTP execution, OpenTelemetry client spans, and Toxiproxy-injected faults, verified state reduced mean regret from 8,956 ms to 0 ms (zero excess observable operational cost) and completed the live action in 9/9 model-by-fault cases versus 5/9 for the neutral control. These studies establish the tools-and-network instance of Agent Harness Awareness: selected host telemetry materially improves pre-dispatch operational choice. Runtime state, hardware pressure, economics, retry-aware recovery, and heterogeneous selection remain open empirical extensions of the same architecture.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Resource Orchestration for Agentic AI Systems
text: Title: Uncertainty-Aware Resource Orchestration for Agentic AI Systems Masoud Shokrnezhad , Tarik Taleb Comments: 6 pages, 2 figures. Accepted to IEEE MECOM 2026, Marrakech, Morocco, 2-4 November 2026 Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI) Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems powered by large language models (LLMs) execute as autonomous multi-step pipelines that dynamically invoke tools, integrate observations into memory, and iterate until a task is resolved or a resource budget is exhausted. Unlike classical workflows with fixed graphs, the aggregate compute, bandwidth, and end-to-end latency demands of such pipelines are unknown at dispatch time: they emerge at runtime from intermediate observations and stochastic token sampling, yielding heavy-tailed, multi-modal random variables. This unpredictability forces infrastructure orchestrators into a dilemma: under-provisioning risks mid-execution throttling and deadline violations, while over-provisioning wastes scarce edge or cloud capacity. Existing schedulers require a fully known pipeline graph, while edge resource-management methods rely on parametric or stationary demand models, and neither fits the unknown, non-stationary profiles of agentic pipelines. We formalize this setting as the uncertainty-aware agentic orchestration problem, where the goal is to reserve, at dispatch time, compute and bandwidth allocations that cover actual pipeline demands, and to verify that the pipeline can meet its deadline, each with a prescribed probability. We then propose Conformal Reservation for Orchestration (CRO), an online algorithm that translates a sliding window of past execution traces into dispatch-time resource allocations with finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees via conformal prediction. Simulations over heterogeneous task mixes with multi-modal and heavy-tailed profiles show that CRO is the only evaluated method that simultaneously satisfies target probabilistic coverage across all risk levels while, among coverage-feasible methods, attaining the lowest over-reservation, roughly halving the resource waste of the Chebyshev-bound baseline.

title: Challenge-Aware Knowledge Recruitment with Meta-Agent Supervision for Medical Multi-Agent Reasoning
text: Title: Challenge-Aware Knowledge Recruitment with Meta-Agent Supervision for Medical Multi-Agent Reasoning Riccardo Riccio , Haitz Sáez de Ocáriz Borde , Pietro Liò Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (cs.LG) Large language models perform strongly on standard medical QA but degrade on harder reasoning tasks, where multi-agent debate often fails to beat strong single-model prompting. We argue that a key limitation is that existing systems select experts and retrieve knowledge from the question alone, rather than from gaps that emerge during reasoning. We propose challenge-aware adaptive recruitment: an external CHALLENGER inspects the evolving reasoning trace and identifies specific factual or expertise gaps. These signals trigger targeted knowledge retrieval or mid-discussion specialist recruitment. On the MEDAGENTSBENCH hard subset (862 questions across nine biomedical datasets), upfront retrieval provides little benefit, while challenge-aware in-between retrieval performs better; on a multi-specialist backbone it improves accuracy on 8 of 9 datasets and adds 6 percentage points over Challenger Only. Ablations indicate benefits from both retrieval timing and gap-specific query signals, and a live web-search experiment shows that the timing advantage persists across retrieval backends. For specialist recruitment, self-triggered adaptation is unreliable, whereas Challenger-triggered recruitment raises GPT-4.1-mini MedQA accuracy from 46% to 54%, with positive direction on all tested generalization datasets. Naively combining retrieval and specialist recruitment degrades performance, highlighting the need to coordinate adaptive intervention channels. These results show that when and why external resources are recruited is a key design choice in multi-agent medical reasoning.

title: A Feasibility Condition for Confidence-Gated Tiered LLM Inference
text: Title: A Feasibility Condition for Confidence-Gated Tiered LLM Inference Sumit P. Ahuja Comments: 21 pages, 2 figures Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Performance (cs.PF) Tiered inference distributes large language model computation across a hierarchy of devices, from on-device and edge hardware to the datacenter, and is increasingly offered as the route to cheaper, lower-latency, and more private serving. Most such systems orchestrate frozen model checkpoints, and most decide what to resolve locally and what to escalate using a confidence signal produced by a forward-deployed model. We give a closed-form condition for when no threshold on that signal makes a tiered cascade worthwhile relative to sending every query to the backstop. Modeling the routing decision as a binary test and separating local from escalation cost through an architecture cost ratio $\kappa$, we derive a feasibility condition bracketed by a signal-free floor, below which a cascade is feasible at any signal quality, and a perfect-signal ceiling, above which none is. Read along the $\kappa$ axis the condition inverts: where local compute is billed, cost binds, matching a recent empirical finding; where it is sunk, on decentralized hardware, feasibility becomes unconditional and signal quality instead sets what the cascade achieves. We turn the condition into three design requirements that existing trained-in primitives satisfy only in isolation, and we propose, as future work, a co-designed architecture and a protocol to test it. The condition and the inversion hold independently of that architecture; they are the paper's contribution.

title: Ranking and Unranking Permutations in Heap's Order
text: Title: Ranking and Unranking Permutations in Heap's Order Yusheng Hu Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS) Heap's algorithm is a permutation generation method with very low constant overhead. Its element-interchanging mechanism, however, prevents the standard factorial-base Lehmer code from being applied directly, and to our knowledge no explicit Rank/Unrank algorithm for the Heap order has been published. This paper describes the block structure of Heap's algorithm in terms of rearrangement operators: the net effect of a block-internal traversal is a tail-preserving operator and the block-boundary swap is a top-level swap operator, and together they yield a closed-form recurrence for the block transitions. On this basis a bottom-up Unrank algorithm and a top-down Rank algorithm are built from one and the same closed-form in-block mapping; both run in $O(n^3)$ time and $O(n)$ space and require no factorial-scale precomputed table. The supporting proofs use a synchronized strong induction on the dimension to establish the bijectivity of the trailing-element mapping, closed forms for the final arrangement and for the trailing sequence, the dichotomy of its cycle structure, and the reciprocity of Rank and Unrank. The Heap order is in fact the colex order of the mixed-radix code.

title: Visual Forensic Detection of Fabricated Bangla News Photocards using Deep Learning
text: Title: Visual Forensic Detection of Fabricated Bangla News Photocards using Deep Learning Anindya Kundu , Kabya Mithun Saha , Md. Muhaiminul Islam , Fayek Ahmed , Aminul Kader Bulbul , Muhammad Ibrahim Comments: 15 pages, 9 figures, 22 tables Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) In Bangladesh, much localized misinformation spreads as photocards: single-image news summaries that imitate the branding of well-known news organizations. Because the misleading message lives in the pixels rather than in machine-readable text, text-based fact-checking tools cannot see it. We recast photocard fake-news detection as visual image forgery detection. We build a dataset of 969 authentic and 1,077 fabricated Bangla photocards scraped from public Facebook pages: authentic cards from the verified pages of seventeen national television broadcasters, fabricated ones from pseudo-broadcaster pages, anonymous profiles, and public groups. Sixteen photometric and morphological transformations per image grow the corpus to 32,736 samples. A fully connected ANN reaches only about 52% accuracy, its loss stuck at ln(2) ~ 0.693, showing that flattening the image destroys the spatial cues forgery detection needs. A compact, fully batch-normalized four-block CNN with 489,954 parameters, about 1,644x smaller than the ANN, is evaluated with leakage-free stratified group five-fold cross-validation, which keeps every augmented version of a card in one fold. Under this protocol the CNN reaches 87.45% +/- 0.53% pooled accuracy from scratch and 88.75% +/- 1.55% when its classifier head is warm-started from the ANN. An ImageNet-pretrained YOLOv8n-cls backbone (1.44M parameters) fine-tuned on the same folds reaches 97.36% +/- 0.42%, marking the headroom above the compact model. We report per-class precision, recall, F1, and pooled confusion matrices, diagnose and fix a one-class collapse caused by an unnormalized classifier head, and give a manual error analysis and bias-variance diagnosis showing that the compact CNNs under-fit.

title: mmHand: Toward Pixel-Level-Accuracy Hand Localization Using a Single Commodity mmWave Device
text: Title: mmHand: Toward Pixel-Level-Accuracy Hand Localization Using a Single Commodity mmWave Device Xiaoyu Zhang , Zhengxiong Li , Chenhan Xu , Luchuan Song , Huining Li , Hongfei Xue , Yingxiao Wu , Wenyao Xu Journal-ref: IEEE Internet of Things Journal, vol. 12, no. 12, pp. 20800-20814, 2025 Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) The hand localization problem has been a longstanding focus due to its many applications. The task involves modeling the hand as a singular point and determining its position within a defined coordinate system. However, due to data modality limitations, existing hand localization technologies face several challenges. For example, vision-based localization raises privacy concerns, while wearable-based methods compromise user comfort. In this paper, we introduce mmHand, a new device-free, privacy-preserving dynamic hand localization system with pixel-level accuracy, using a single commodity mmWave device. We first propose a mmImage generation tool to fully extract spatial information from raw mmWave data and introduce a novel 2D image-format representation of mmWave data. Next, we design a framework that provides a new quality evaluation method and pixel space labeling for the mmWave data. Finally, we present a cross-modality spatial feature-enhanced model with high spatial feature extraction capabilities, which can accurately localize hand positions at the pixel level in the mmWave radar U-V pixel coordinate system. We evaluate the system with experiments on 12 subjects in three scenarios, and the results across four metrics demonstrate the effectiveness of our hand localization system.

title: When Does Sharing Work? Scaling a Shared SigLIP2 Across Image, Video, Audio, and Audio-Visual Representations
text: Title: When Does Sharing Work? Scaling a Shared SigLIP2 Across Image, Video, Audio, and Audio-Visual Representations Xiaofei Sun , Peng Wang , Huayao Liu , Xiaoxiao Xu , Jun Song , Deqing Li , Lin Qu Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) Contrastive pretraining has advanced image-text understanding, yet image, video, and audio encoders are still trained independently, with cross-modal alignment realized mainly through post-hoc binding to a frozen anchor space. We present Omni-Encoder, a general multimodal encoder that processes image, video, audio, and audio-visual inputs within a single SigLIP-2 Vision Transformer with fully shared parameters. Unlike anchor-centric binding or per-modality adapters, all modalities are optimized jointly end-to-end, and the framework is organized from input to training. A modality-native input stage first maps each signal into the shared embedding space, including a 1D-convolutional audio tokenizer that converts mel-spectrograms into tokens aligned with visual patches. A multimodal rotary position embedding parameterized by absolute timestamps then places visual frames and audio segments in a unified spatiotemporal coordinate system. Finally, alternating-modality training interleaves image, video, audio, and temporally aligned audio-visual batches and accumulates their gradients into one update, which we find central to stable joint optimization. Omni-Encoder achieves competitive results on 16 benchmarks across all four modalities with one shared parameter set, and joint training improves each modality over its separately trained counterpart. Code and models will be publicly released.

title: PEEK: One-Step-Look-Ahead Exposure Bias Correction for Diffusion Sampling
text: Title: PEEK: One-Step-Look-Ahead Exposure Bias Correction for Diffusion Sampling Yunwei Bai , Ying Kiat Tan , Tsuhan Chen Comments: Accepted to Neurips 2026 Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) Diffusion image generators are successful due to accurate denoising networks and strong numerical samplers. Yet the two components are not fully matched. During sampling, the denoiser predicts for the next step based on flawed input that differ much from the real data. This train-test gap, or exposure bias, caps image generation quality (i.e., blurry, lacking in details or awkward in shape). To mitigate the problem, we propose PEEK, a novel training-free deterministic sampler plugin. At each eligible denoising step, PEEK first performs a provisional one-step update, evaluates the denoiser once at the look-ahead state, and interpolates it with the one-step-later prediction to form the next noisy state. By taking the additional step, we obtain a generally more-image-like prediction from the higher-signal noisy state, mitigating the exposure bias. To optimize the interpolation positions, PEEK searches for an interpolation schedule search made efficient by the prefix and baseline noise-schedule-rebasing caches. On 8 pixel-space and latent-space diffusion models with unconditional, label-guided, and text-guided settings across various output resolutions, PEEK consistently improves over NFE-matched baselines, with FID improvements up to 49.3\% at minimal extra computation cost (e.g., the one-time-per-model calibration takes at most 2.2 minutes across our experiments.). Project website is at this https URL .

title: Augmentation with Reinforcement Transformation for Low-textured Scientific Sketch Image Retrieval
text: Title: Augmentation with Reinforcement Transformation for Low-textured Scientific Sketch Image Retrieval Zhiqiang Wang , Sheri L. Barton , Jennifer H. Johnson , Yi He , Xingquan Zhu Comments: IEEE BigData 2026 Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) Low-textured sketch images are widely used in scientific applications, including wildlife conservation, archaeological illustration, and forensic composites. Learning from and retrieving such images is challenging because they lack detailed surface textures and visual variations commonly exploited by modern deep learning models. This paper proposes Augmentation with Reinforcement Transformation (ART) to fine-tune pretrained models to learn effective representations for accurate sketch image retrieval. Our key observation is that sketches are particularly sensitive to image transformations, such as rotation, flipping, zooming, and stretching. While some transformations preserve their structural integrity, others may introduce distortions that hinder representation learning. Instead of randomly choosing transformations to construct fine-tuning views, ART formulates augmentation selection as a multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem, where transformations are treated as arms and their effectiveness is continuously evaluated through rewards. This enables ART to adaptively construct reward-guided view banks before self-supervised fine-tuning; the subsequent representation loss does not feed back to ART. On Florida manatee sketches provided by Mote Marine Laboratory, ART achieves 71.40% average Top-1 accuracy for transformed-scar retrieval, compared with 68.83% for random augmentation selection, and 55.84% for location-aware sketch retrieval, compared with 18.18% for frozen CLIP.

title: PointNDF: Cascaded Neural Displacement Fields for Point Cloud Denoising
text: Title: PointNDF: Cascaded Neural Displacement Fields for Point Cloud Denoising Michael Y. Wang , Pingping Cai Comments: 14 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Accepted to MMM 2027 (33rd International Conference on Multimedia Modeling) Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) Point cloud denoising aims to recover clean geometry from noisy 3D observations while preserving both fine surface details and the underlying spatial distribution of the points. Many learning-based methods adopt a two-stage pipeline that first extracts point-wise features from the noisy input and subsequently predicts point-wise displacements via simple regressions. However, these approaches often lack robust feature guidance and distribution-aware geometric refinement, causing them to fail at maintaining optimal point uniformity and geometric quality. To address these limitations, we propose PointNDF, a denoising framework that combines patch-level geometric context with local displacement prediction. Specifically, a Point Transformer V3 (PTv3) encoder aggregates multiscale geometric information into a global patch descriptor. Rather than directly regressing an unconstrained displacement vector, a Neural Displacement Field (NDF) fuses this global patch descriptor with per-point neighborhood features. It then predicts each displacement through bounded-vector and scale factor branches, thereby achieving a superior, more uniform point distribution. Three cascaded NDF stages propagate local features and progressively refine the point positions. Experiments on PU-Net and ModelNet10 demonstrate competitive denoising accuracy and favorable inference efficiency. The source code is publicly available at this https URL .

title: HippocamPEX: A Hippocampus-Inspired In-Silico Architecture for Context-Aware Sequence Prediction
text: Title: HippocamPEX: A Hippocampus-Inspired In-Silico Architecture for Context-Aware Sequence Prediction Md Abdullah al Kaiser , Keiland W. Cooper , Rouhan Noor , Ankur Singh , Zhishun Yang , Hamed Poursiami , Bhuvanesh Sathish Kayarabettu , Ziyi Liang , Babak Shahbaba , Maryam Parsa , Norbert J. Fortin , Akhilesh Jaiswal Comments: 6 figures Subjects: Hardware Architecture (cs.AR) The brain's hippocampus enables episodic memory - the ability to encode events within their context, organize them into sequences, and generate predictive representations to guide adaptive behavior. Modern computing architectures, however, are optimized for large-scale arithmetic and struggle with such context-dependent sequential prediction or "cognitive" tasks. To translate these capabilities into a mixed-signal architecture, we first derived a working model from the neuroscience literature distilling key hippocampal computations into engineering-friendly abstractions. We then leveraged converging advances in in-memory computing, neuromorphic computing, asynchronous circuits, and analog computing to design a mixed-signal hardware architecture implementing these computations, called HippocamPEX. Finally, we demonstrated that HippocamPEX reproduces characteristic representational dynamics of hippocampal subregions and performs robust context-specific sequence prediction through detailed activity and circuit simulations. By tightly coupling hardware design with neuroscience knowledge, this work establishes a pathway for artificial systems capable of rapid, adaptive, and context-aware decision-making, addressing a central gap between biological and conventional computing.

title: Unlocking Turing Tensor Cores: A Measured Throughput Account of From-Scratch Pre-training on a Single 22G RTX 2080 Ti
text: Title: Unlocking Turing Tensor Cores: A Measured Throughput Account of From-Scratch Pre-training on a Single 22G RTX 2080 Ti Dezhou Shen Comments: 7 pages, 4 tables Subjects: Hardware Architecture (cs.AR) ; Computation and Language (cs.CL); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Performance (cs.PF) The RTX 2080 Ti (TU102) ships full second-generation Tensor Cores in hardware, yet the vendor throttles FP16 matrix multiplication at the driver level, leaving usable tensor throughput well below the hardware peak. turing-unlock lifts this restriction with a kernel module that, before the nvidia driver binds the device, writes the FP16 speed selectors (SS0=0x88888888, SS1=0x8) and releases the ACR mutex; published measurements report cuBLAS FP16 matmul throughput rising from 55.7 to 91.4 TFLOPS (about 1.6x). On the same 22G 2080 Ti and under the same from-scratch pre-training protocol as the companion memory ledger (five tiers of Chinese encoder-decoder models, 2,451 steps per tier, 16,384 tokens per step, seed 42), we obtain a before/after throughput account: the small tier (75.7M parameters, 512-wide, 8+8 layers, activation checkpointing on) improves in steady-state throughput from 6,480 to 7,246 tok/s (+11.8%) with wall time cut from 1.77h to 1.61h (9.0% saved); the tiny tier goes from 15,150 to 15,866 tok/s (+4.7%) with wall time savings of 3.8%; the three smaller tiers (pico-micro) gain at most +0.3%; per-tier peak memory stays bit-identical, and final quality metrics are bit-identical or consistent within 10^-3. We conclude that the unlock gain is a function of matrix size, rising monotonically with tier -- imperceptible for pico-micro, visible from tiny upward, and cashed out as a double-digit percentage at small -- and that it is a pure throughput gain that leaves training dynamics untouched.

title: CAST-Bench: Tracing Every Sound to Its Source in Multi-Shot Audio-Video Generation
text: Title: CAST-Bench: Tracing Every Sound to Its Source in Multi-Shot Audio-Video Generation Yucong Liu , Qi Tian , Shuyuan Tu , Kaihang Pan , Weijie Kong , Chao Pan Comments: 9 pages ,6 figures Subjects: Sound (cs.SD) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) Existing benchmarks for joint text-to-audio-video (T2AV) generation evaluate perceptual quality and audiovisual alignment, but balanced sound-source sam?pling and separate reporting by shot structure remain limited. This makes it dif?ficult to determine whether a specific sound is missing, attributed to the wrong source, or lost across shot transitions. To address this, we introduce CAST?BENCH, a benchmark designed to trace every generated sound back to its in?tended source in multi-shot audio-video generation. The core idea is to formu?late T2AV correctness as an audiovisual contract in which each requested sound must be emitted by the right source, synchronized with the corresponding visual action, and carry the right semantic content. Concretely, the benchmark orga?nizes 900 prompts into 9 sound-source categories, with 100 prompts per cate?gory, spanning speech, animals, instruments, ambient sounds, and other emitter types. The prompts include 439 single-shot and 461 multi-shot narratives, each derived from a structured specification that links every audio event to its emit?ter, subject, and temporal slot. The benchmark provides an 18-metric evaluation suite covering three dimensions: Visual Performance, Content Consistency, and Audio & Semantic Alignment. We further benchmark 12 representative gen?erators and find that visual quality is nearly saturated across leading systems, yet audio semantic scores still differ markedly. Across the nine shared mod?els, multi-shot prompts receive lower aggregate scores under the subset-specific scoring rules and yield different model rankings. Multi-person speech, con?sistent speaker identity across shots, and cross-shot event retention remain the main unresolved challenges. All prompts and evaluation code are available at this https URL .

title: LLM-based NPCs in Video Games: A Systematic Mapping Study
text: Title: LLM-based NPCs in Video Games: A Systematic Mapping Study Dilan Mian , Jeremy Bradbury , Yann-Gaël Guéhéneuc , Fabio Petrillo , Cristiano Politowski Comments: 12 pages. Accepted manuscript. Published in IEEE Transactions on Games (Early Access) Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) For decades, non-player characters (NPCs) have been driven by rule-based systems whose personalities and interactions are scripted before release. Large language models (LLMs) promise NPCs that converse openly, adapt to new situations, and behave in ways developers did not fully author, prompting a wave of research and commercial experimentation. Yet the field lacks a unified picture of what has been built, how well it works, and at what cost. We address this gap with a systematic mapping study of 377 papers from the academic literature, yielding 42 papers analysed against a main research question and ten sub-questions across four thematic axes. We provide the first quantitative characterisation of component adoption, latency, safety coverage, and reproducibility: short-term memory and world-state grounding are near-universal (60% and 69%), whereas long-term memory (31%), reflection (38%), and retrieval-augmented generation (14%) remain rare, and response times span 2.6 to 15 seconds. Finally, we identify six structural barriers to commercial adoption and offer evidence-based recommendations for developers and researchers.

title: On the most informative Boolean function under noise
text: Title: On the most informative Boolean function under noise Dimiter Kramer , Mert Saglam Comments: 17 pages, 2 figures Subjects: Information Theory (cs.IT) ; Combinatorics (math.CO) Let $X$ be a uniform random bit string and $Y$ be obtained by flipping each bit of $X$ independently with probability $p$. Let $C$ be a random bit obtained as a function of $Y$. We show that $\mathbf{I}(C:X)\le \mathbf{I}(Y_1:X)$ for all $p\in[0,1]$, which resolves a conjecture posed by Courtade and Kumar in 2013.

title: Constraint-Preserving Flow Matching for Spectral Graph Generation
text: Title: Constraint-Preserving Flow Matching for Spectral Graph Generation Anita Yang , Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi , Yohan Jung Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) Spectral graph generation models graphs through the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of their Laplacians, providing a compact and continuous alternative to direct graph construction. However, these eigensystems must retain the structural properties of graph Laplacians. Existing approaches preserve eigenvector orthonormality but do not enforce the Laplacian nullspace constraint, potentially producing eigensystems inconsistent with Laplacian structure. To address this, we introduce Laplacian-Constrained Stiefel Flow Matching (LaSFM), which preserves the nullspace condition alongside eigenvector orthonormality and positive eigenvalues during generation. We characterize the underlying constrained Stiefel manifold and formulate flow matching on it. We further extend LaSFM to property-guided generation, steering samples toward desired graph properties while maintaining these constraints. Experiments demonstrate improved performance on both spectral and graph-level metrics, along with better alignment with target properties.

title: Req-Space: A User Study of Interactive Visualisations for Requirements Review
text: Title: Req-Space: A User Study of Interactive Visualisations for Requirements Review Risha Parveen , Navneet Arora , Zheying Zhang , Kalle Mäkelä , Pekka Abrahamsson Comments: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE) Requirements review involves identifying inconsistencies and assessing change implications across distributed specifications. Motivated by needs raised in industrial project workshops, we investigate Req-Space, an interactive prototype integrating semantic exploration and traceability visualisation to support human-led review. We conducted a fixed-order, two-phase study with 20 participants, including 11 with at least three years of software or IT experience. Participants reviewed a fictional 40-requirement software specification and a guest-checkout change request, first using source documents and then revisiting the same tasks with Req-Space. During the supported review, 17 participants recorded at least one additional source-supported item or pair. Of 69 assessable additional units, 58 (84.1%) were judged supported by the source materials. Seven decision rationales were judged stronger in Phase 2, including five without a change in the decision category. Participants generally found the visualisations helpful, although workload responses were mixed and some misinterpreted visual relationships. The findings suggest that visual support can facilitate requirements exploration and decision justification, provided relationship meanings and source context remain clear. The fixed study sequence prevents attributing the observed changes specifically to Req-Space.

title: Learning Implicit Solves for Dynamic Simulations
text: Title: Learning Implicit Solves for Dynamic Simulations Chawit Kaewnuratchadasorn , Jiaji Wang , Xin Nie Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Computational Engineering, Finance, and Science (cs.CE) High-fidelity simulation of dynamical systems is central to scientific discovery and engineering design, yet remains computationally demanding. Here we introduce the Implicit Neural Operator Solver (INOS), which learns the implicit solve and encodes a time integrator. INOS pretrains a neural operator from static equilibrium solutions and reuses it within Newmark-$\beta$ integration. At each time increment, the integrator forms an effective equilibrium problem, the pretrained neural operator infers the next-step solution field, and the Newmark relations advance the dynamic state. Numerical examples in linear and nonlinear elastodynamics demonstrate accurate full-field predictions without dynamic trajectory supervision. Comparative results show that INOS, evaluated zero-shot, achieves higher predictive accuracy than neural solver baselines trained on dynamic simulations. In addition, INOS delivers over 4,600$\times$ speedup in nonlinear simulations over sequential classical finite-element solvers. INOS natively accommodates changes in dynamic conditions and enables reuse of the pretrained operator across spatial and temporal discretizations. Further evaluation demonstrates a stable million-step rollout. These findings establish INOS as a reusable neural implicit solver for accurate, efficient, and robust dynamic modeling.

title: Matched but Not Better: An Equivalence-Tested Benchmark of Quantum Machine Learning on Six Clinical Datasets and the QML-Health-READY Reporting Framework
text: Title: Matched but Not Better: An Equivalence-Tested Benchmark of Quantum Machine Learning on Six Clinical Datasets and the QML-Health-READY Reporting Framework Mohammed Siraj B , Gousia Habib , Ruban S Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) Background: Quantum machine learning (QML) is promoted for clinical prediction, but comparisons with classical models are rarely paired or tested for equivalence. Methods: We compared a quantum-kernel support vector machine (QSVM; 4 qubits, tuned bandwidth) and a variational quantum classifier (VQC) with five tuned classical models across six public clinical datasets. All models used identical four-component inputs and 25 cross-validation splits. Paired AUROC differences were assessed using a corrected resampled t-test, Holm-adjusted equivalence tests (margins: +/-0.02 and +/-0.05), and random-effects pooling. Ablation, noise, finite-shot, and implementation-fault analyses were conducted. We propose QML-Health-READY, an eight-domain reporting framework. Results: Neither quantum model significantly outperformed any classical comparator. Pooled across datasets, QSVM differed from the kernel-matched radial basis function (RBF) SVM by -0.006 AUROC (95% CI: -0.017 to +0.004), equivalent to +/-0.02. VQC differed from the best classical model by -0.007 (95% CI: -0.019 to +0.004). QSVM was equivalent to RBF SVM within +/-0.05 in four of six datasets but was significantly worse than the best classical model on NHANES 2017-18 (-0.076). A classically trivial product-state kernel performed as well as the entangling kernel. With depolarizing noise (p = 0.01) and 1,024 shots per kernel entry, QSVM AUROC decreased by 0.054 (95% CI: 0.036 to 0.071). Untuned bandwidth produced near-chance AUROC (0.48-0.59). Conclusions: Correctly configured quantum classifiers approached but did not exceed tuned classical models. Finite-shot estimation, rather than gate noise, was their main practical cost, while configuration errors could reverse conclusions. QML-Health-READY defines reporting requirements for credible claims.

title: SurgTransfer: Multi-Step Latent Action Modeling for Action Transfer in Surgical World Model
text: Title: SurgTransfer: Multi-Step Latent Action Modeling for Action Transfer in Surgical World Model Saurabh Koju , Love Panta , Deepak Thapa , Rudra P. K. Poudel , Prajwal Ghimire , Angus Watson , Yash Raj Shrestha , Prashnna Kumar Gyawali , Binod Bhattarai Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG) Surgical world models have the potential to provide intra-operative guidance, accelerate risk-free training and facilitate transfer of expert surgical maneuvers. However, the use of world models for transferring surgical expertise has been largely unexplored. Moreover, recent approaches in this domain have mainly relied on ground truth kinematics actions or expert annotations for specific tasks, limiting their applicability beyond the narrow range of tasks with ground-truth annotations. In contrast, existing works in the natural domain have shown promising results in learning latent actions solely from unlabeled videos and transferring the learned actions across contexts. We observe that this paradigm is short-sighted for the surgical domain, failing to capture the hierarchical and goal-directed structure of surgical procedures. Thus, we propose a novel multi-step action learning framework to learn context-invariant latent actions that are easily transferable across various surgical contexts. We perform extensive experiments on the publicly available datasets, SurgToolLoc-2022 and PitVis-2023, verifying our approach with both quantitative metrics and qualitative evaluation by surgical experts. We have published our code and the implementation details at this https URL .

title: LIBRA: Programmatic Induction of Executable Tool Libraries
text: Title: LIBRA: Programmatic Induction of Executable Tool Libraries Zekai Li , Zhenke Liu , Yonghao Li , Junhan Liu , Xulong Xiao , Jiapeng Zhang Comments: 10 pages, 5 figures. Introduces LIBRA, a query-agnostic tool library built via execution-validated prerequisites in a sandbox (avg ARR review score: 3.5/5). Demonstrates consistent performance gains across three benchmarks while discussing sandbox dependencies and library construction trade-offs Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Information Retrieval (cs.IR) Large language model agents increasingly retrieve tools from large catalogs, yet most retrievers rank each tool independently by request similarity. For multi tool tasks, this recovers the goal matching tool while omitting prerequisite tools required by the this http URL introduce LIBRA, a framework for Library Induction by Runtime Assembly that turns a flat tool catalog into an executable tool library. An LLM proposes per tool contracts of candidate invocations, reusable outputs and state changes, and success conditions; LIBRA then tests these compositions in a sandbox and retains the relations supported at runtime. Constructed before user queries, the library requires no dependency annotations, tool use trajectories, or task specific training, and supports both one-shot and agentic retrieval. On AppWorld, BFCL, and SciToolEval, LIBRA improves one-shot Recall and NDCG over the same dense retriever by 7.9 and 3.7 percentage points on average. Within ToolReAGt, it yields corresponding gains of 4.5 and 2.9 points after ten retrieval iterations.

title: A Fully Polynomial Approximation Algorithm for the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick Model
text: Title: A Fully Polynomial Approximation Algorithm for the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick Model Dylan Herman , Shouvanik Chakrabarti , Junhyung Lyle Kim , Guneykan Ozgul Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS) ; Statistical Mechanics (cond-mat.stat-mech); Optimization and Control (math.OC); Probability (math.PR); Quantum Physics (quant-ph) Montanari's incremental approximate message passing (IAMP) algorithm [FOCS 2019; SIAM J. Comput., 2025] and the zero-temperature formulation of El Alaoui, Montanari and Sellke (AMS) [Ann. Probab., 2021] find a $(1-\varepsilon)$ approximation to the maximum Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) energy in $C(\varepsilon)N^2$ operations for fixed accuracy, with probability tending to one as $N\to\infty$, under their respective full-support and access-model assumptions. However, it was unknown whether this approximation could be achieved with work polynomial in both $N$ and $1/\varepsilon$, together with quantitative guarantees at finite dimension. Under the same assumptions as AMS, we introduce grouped IAMP with exact Gaussian query outputs (GEG-IAMP), which is the first SK approximation algorithm with total work polynomial in $N$ and $1/\varepsilon$ and a finite-size guarantee above a dimension threshold polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$ and $\log(1/\alpha)$. More precisely, for every $\alpha\in(0,1/2)$, it returns a $(1-\varepsilon)$ approximation with probability at least $1-\alpha$ whenever $N\ge \mathsf{K}\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2(e/\varepsilon)\log(\mathsf{K}/\alpha)$, using $O(N^2/\varepsilon)$ work and $O(N^2)$ storage. GEG-IAMP replaces the Onsager correction by Reeves's coupling construction [ arXiv:2508.10782 ] and groups Euler-Maruyama steps into $O(1/\varepsilon)$ matrix-vector products. We also prove a relative guarantee for AMS IAMP with $O(N^2\varepsilon^{-3}\log^2(e/\varepsilon))$ work but a sufficient dimension exponential in inverse accuracy. By returning a fixed configuration below its dimension threshold, GEG-IAMP also provides an asymptotic fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme (AFPRAS), with an additive error independent of dimension.

title: Jev with Foresight: Safe Language-Guided Autonomous Driving via a Language World Model
text: Title: Jev with Foresight: Safe Language-Guided Autonomous Driving via a Language World Model Yansong Qu , Jiancong Chen , Samuel Labi Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) Large language models understand passengers' driving commands, but as driving agents they reason in generated text for seconds and must infer each action's consequences implicitly from the scene. We present Jev-AD, which pairs Jev, a typed decision model that answers predefined questions with probabilities, not generated text, with a language world model that predicts for every candidate action how nearby vehicles move over the next two seconds. Code turns these predictions into foreseen consequences, which Jev compares instead of inferring them from coordinates. In simulated highway merging (500 car-episodes), this foresight lowers the same decision model's collision rate from 26.0% to 2.4% at 0.25 seconds per decision, and Jev-AD achieves the passenger's intent in 93% of free-form command trials. In 500 replayed real-world NGSIM episodes, foresight lowers the collision rate from 48.2% to 2.8%, and the world model, learned from this traffic, foresees 93% of dangerous actions. Project page: this https URL .

title: SO(3)-Equivariant Learning on CAD Boundary Representations
text: Title: SO(3)-Equivariant Learning on CAD Boundary Representations Matteo Ballegeer , Dries F. Benoit Comments: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 main track Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG) Learning on boundary representations (B-reps) requires robustness to the pose of a part, since CAD models are not stored in a canonical orientation. Existing B-rep networks either operate on world-frame coordinates and normals, and thus degrade under rotation, or encode each face in a local reference frame. Local frames yield invariance, but reduce inter-face messages to scalars and discard the relative orientation of adjacent faces. We propose SO3brep, an SO(3)-equivariant graph neural network on the B-rep face-adjacency graph. Node features are computed in local frames and mapped into a shared frame by Wigner D-matrices. Clebsch-Gordan tensor products couple these features with the directions between adjacent faces, so that relative orientation is preserved throughout message passing and the output remains SE(3)-invariant. Across three face-segmentation and two classification benchmarks with randomly rotated test parts, SO3brep achieves the highest accuracy among the compared B-rep networks and equivariant point cloud networks, with the fewest parameters. Its advantage is largest with few labeled parts, a setting typical of industrial CAD. Code is available at this https URL .

title: Towards Robust Long-Lived Agents: Benchmarking Experience Lifecycles in Evolving Environments
text: Title: Towards Robust Long-Lived Agents: Benchmarking Experience Lifecycles in Evolving Environments Shijue Huang , Hangyu Guo , Hengheng Zhang , Guo An , Zhitao He , Qi Tian , Yiren Feng Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) As agents become more capable, they are moving beyond one-off tasks toward sustained assistance across successive user goals. Such assistance requires agents to discover how unfamiliar environments work, reuse what they learn across tasks, and keep that experience current as environments evolve. Existing benchmarks increasingly study experience reuse and adaptation, but provide limited insight into which parts of accumulated experience agents revise, retain, or lose. To address this gap, we introduce ReScopeBench, a benchmark for the experience lifecycle across 18 interactive environments. It distinguishes structural experience about how an environment is organized and accessed from rule experience about reusable principles and constraints that guide decisions across tasks. To study how experience is acquired, reused, and revised, we propose an experience-first construction approach. It builds task streams around shared experience and introduces silent environmental changes. We evaluate task performance and track changes in saved experience throughout each stream. Across 20 models, we find that retained experience improves task performance, but agents struggle to keep it current as environments change. Even when the required experience is correctly recorded, agents do not always complete tasks successfully. These findings identify selective maintenance and effective use as complementary challenges for long-lived agents.

title: From Tokens to Trajectories: Parameter-Efficient Continuous Adaptation of Unified Multimodal Models
text: Title: From Tokens to Trajectories: Parameter-Efficient Continuous Adaptation of Unified Multimodal Models Gayatri Deshmukh , Onkar Susladkar , Adheesh Juvekar , Halil Kilicoglu , Ismini Lourentzou Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) While discrete tokenization in Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) establishes strong semantic reasoning, it introduces a strict quantization bottleneck that degrades fine-grained visual details, often resulting in structurally accurate but artifact-heavy images. We introduce FlowShift, a parameter-efficient post-training framework that bypasses this bottleneck by converting pre-trained discrete UMMs into continuous rectified-flow generators. Instead of discarding the backbone's semantic priors, FlowShift replaces discrete visual interfaces with continuous latent projections and applies LoRA to the attention layers. To efficiently boost visual quality without semantic drift, we propose Dual-Objective Velocity Vector Distillation (DOVD), which aligns the model with a high-fidelity continuous teacher and ground-truth continuous trajectories. This approach drastically improves perceptual quality while preserving prompt adherence and reasoning. When applied to leading discrete UMMs, FlowShift significantly improves COCO-30K FID and aesthetic scores, while retaining over 99.5% of multimodal understanding capabilities. Ablations confirm DOVD drives generation quality. Ultimately, FlowShift achieves high-fidelity continuous generation without sacrificing pre-trained semantic grounding.

title: Agentic Behavior Engineering: A Design-by-Contract Methodology for Specifying, Verifying, and Governing Enterprise AI Agents
text: Title: Agentic Behavior Engineering: A Design-by-Contract Methodology for Specifying, Verifying, and Governing Enterprise AI Agents Yang Song Comments: 30 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables. Expanded version of the author's practitioner guide "Agentic behavior engineering" in the Microsoft Azure Architecture Center (CC BY 4.0): this https URL Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE) Enterprise teams that deploy large language model (LLM) agents inherit a maintenance problem that traditional testing does not address. The model is non-deterministic, but the larger risk is that most of what changes an agent's behavior (a retired model version, a revised policy, an upstream schema change, a prompt edit meant to fix one case) originates outside the owning team and is discovered as a production defect rather than caught as a regression. This paper presents Agentic Behavior Engineering (ABE), a platform-agnostic methodology that treats observable agent behavior, rather than the prompt or the model, as the version-controlled engineering artifact. ABE adapts Design by Contract to non-deterministic systems. A specification-only behavior contract with stable rule identifiers states what the agent must do, must not do, and when it must abstain for lack of evidence; a lightweight scenario library turns each rule into concrete situations; and every engineering artifact (tests, runtime policies, telemetry) references the contract in one direction only, so that specification and implementation can change independently without drifting apart. The method organizes the work into five responsibilities (Specify, Ground, Control, Verify, Observe), treats missing evidence and a verified negative as different things, enforces authority outside the model, gates releases on per-scenario pass^k reliability rather than aggregate accuracy, and classifies every production run against the contract so that each finding routes to the asset that must change. We illustrate the method with an executable capacity-allocation boundary suite and a constructed worked example of a product-review approval workflow.

title: Hybrid LLM-Deterministic Pipelines for Enterprise-Scale Code Migration at Bloomberg
text: Title: Hybrid LLM-Deterministic Pipelines for Enterprise-Scale Code Migration at Bloomberg Mario Corchero , David Williams , Laszlo Kiss Kollar , Haowen Liu , Shivam Bairoliya , Gala Malbasic , Serkan Kirbas , Federica Sarro Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) Large organizations carry a long tail of infrastructure migrations that are worth doing but rarely urgent enough to compete with feature work, because each one costs significant engineering time per repository. This paper reports on our industrial experience from Automated Uplift, a multi-month initiative applying LLM-assisted migration pipelines across thousands of Bloomberg repositories. We examine two distinct production campaigns: a heterogeneous Python packaging migration (approx. 1,900 candidate repositories) and a uniform C++ build system migration (approx. 6,700 candidate repositories). Together, these campaigns generated 2,333 pull requests, resulting in 729 successful migrations. We detail our hybrid architectural solution which maximizes deterministic processing, confines the LLM to bounded file transformations within a pre-computed context, and incorporates runtime production telemetry (such as execution logs and usage traces). Our findings show that generating migrations turned out to be the easier part; the bottleneck was the cost, for owning teams, of reviewing, testing, and deploying them. These costs were lowered when changes could be verified directly in the pipeline before opening a PR (as with C++ compilation and test validation), and when the population was uniform enough for fixes to carry over from one repository to the next. We conclude by distilling our experience and findings into actionable, transferable patterns for architecting hybrid LLM-deterministic pipelines and scaling code migrations across the enterprise

title: Can Large Language Models Review the Scientific Literature? A Test Against a 102-Article Benchmark
text: Title: Can Large Language Models Review the Scientific Literature? A Test Against a 102-Article Benchmark Abdullah Al Kalbani , David M. Schultz , Alexandra K. Anderson-Frey , Zhonghua Zheng , Catherine McGuire Comments: 34 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Data, prompts, analysis scripts and results: this https URL (GitHub: this https URL ) Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Digital Libraries (cs.DL) Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support scientific literature reviews, yet evaluations often examine individual tasks rather than the review process as a whole. We assess six AI tools across four stages: finding relevant articles, interpreting them, synthesizing across them, and proposing future research. The benchmark is a published review of the Spanish plume weather pattern and its 102-article corpus. In the initial searches, five tools collectively identified 57 articles, with the best individual tool finding 42. Institutional library access increased discovery from 42 to 82 articles for Codex and from 15 to 79 for Claude Code. Given the complete corpus of 102 PDFs, three tools correctly identified all 18 articles discussing the Spanish plume substantially, but incorrectly classified 40% to 79% of the 84 passing mentions as substantial. The same three tools produced syntheses evaluated blindly by two domain experts. Although largely accurate, the syntheses provided limited insight and sometimes contained unsupported claims, quotation errors, and exaggerated statements of consensus. Finally, all three tools proposed research directions broader than the Spanish plume literature, although two approached questions identified in the benchmark review. No single tool performed best across all tasks. We provide eight recommendations for researchers using AI tools in literature reviews. Our findings suggest that LLMs can assist with discovering and interpreting scientific literature, particularly when institutional access is available, but cannot replace expert judgment in evaluating evidence or synthesizing research.

title: The Power and Limits of Money Burning in Bilateral Trade
text: Title: The Power and Limits of Money Burning in Bilateral Trade Moshe Babaioff , Noam Nisan , Ariel Shaulker Subjects: Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT) We study the power of money burning in bilateral trade. In this problem, a seller owns an indivisible item, a buyer would like to acquire it, and each of these two traders has a private value for the item and the values are sampled from independent distributions. We ask whether the traders can benefit from a mechanism that burns money, that is, one that charges the buyer more than it pays the seller, so that neither trader enjoys the difference (money burnt is a loss for the traders). Is it possible that the traders will ever be better off if the trade mechanism can burn money? For Bayesian incentive-compatible mechanisms and for deterministic dominant-strategy incentive-compatible (DSIC) mechanisms, it is known that money burning is always a waste and can only hurt the traders. Maybe surprisingly, we show that once a DSIC mechanism can use randomization, money burning can significantly benefit the traders, and the gain of each of them can be arbitrarily large. In contrast, we show that the power of DSIC randomized mechanisms that burn money is still very limited in the sense that they cannot guarantee any constant fraction of the first-best gains-from-trade.

title: Objective-Conditioned Active Preference Learning for Multi-Objective Alignment
text: Title: Objective-Conditioned Active Preference Learning for Multi-Objective Alignment Duc Anh Vu , Thong Nguyen , Hoang Pham , Ponhvoan Srey , Luu Anh Tuan Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) Aligning large language models (LLMs) with several objectives, such as helpfulness, harmlessness, and honesty, typically relies on preference judgment for each objective, growing the annotation cost linearly with the number of objectives. Active preference learning can reduce this cost by selecting the comparisons whose labels are expected to change the policy most. Existing remedies either lack an objective-aware query selection mechanism for the multi-objective setting or regard conflicting preferences as harmful, therefore excluding them from the training data. We introduce OGC-DPO (Objective-conditioned Gradient Coverage DPO), an active learning framework that treats each (response pair, objective) combination as a separate query and measures its informativeness through the policy's own implicit gradient, without relying on an external reward model. OGC-DPO then selects the queries that most expand each objective's gradient coverage. Empirical experiments across varying numbers of objectives demonstrate the effectiveness of OGC-DPO over existing active preference learning methods under the same annotation cost. Further analysis demonstrates that informative conflicts, rather than being uniformly harmful, provide a useful policy training signal.

title: Ctrl-F: Force as an Interface for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
text: Title: Ctrl-F: Force as an Interface for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation Mengjie Zhao , Yuxin Chen , Yiyang Shao , Chuye Hong , Jiakang Chen , Koushil Sreenath , Masayoshi Tomizuka Comments: Project page: this https URL Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG) Humanoid motion tracking has scaled to general policies that reproduce diverse human motion, but the resulting behavior is in free-space: the tracker knows where the body should be, not how it should interact with the environment. Other work makes the object part of the objective, yet abstracts that interaction to contact or geometry, which leaves the demanding cases under-explored. We argue that force is a natural command channel between motion imitation and object interaction, one that specifies not just where to make contact but how hard. We present Ctrl-F, a hierarchical motion-force framework that augments motion tracking with an explicit force command, a 3-D force at each designated contact body such as a hand or a foot. The hierarchical framework comprises: (1) A unified motion-force controller tracks the reference motion while applying the commanded force to the world. (2) A high-level force planner that issues a force command online based on object state and proprioception observations. In simulation and on hardware, Ctrl-F completes loco-manipulation that demands large, sustained interaction force and adjusts its command online as the load changes, both out of reach of a force-blind tracker. On hardware, Ctrl-F demonstrates hand-based dragging, pushing, and lifting, as well as foot-based kicking, successfully manipulating boxes weighing up to 20kg in pushing and kicking tasks where the force-blind baseline fails, while adapting online to additional loads introduced mid-task.

title: Improved lower bounds on the approximability of Multiway Cut using Sherali-Adams relaxations
text: Title: Improved lower bounds on the approximability of Multiway Cut using Sherali-Adams relaxations Joshua Brakensiek , Neng Huang , Aaron Potechin , Uri Zwick Comments: 66 pages Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS) ; Computational Complexity (cs.CC) The Multiway Cut problem is among the most well-studied problems in the area of combinatorial approximation algorithms. The currently best approximation ratio for the problem is 1.2787, obtained recently by the authors (2026). The best lower bound on the approximation ratio that can be achieved for the problem in polynomial time, under the Unique Games Conjecture (UGC), is 1.20016, obtained by Bérczi, Chandrasekaran, Király, and Madan (2020), building on and slightly improving a bound of $\frac65=1.2$, obtained by Angelidakis, Makarychev, and Manurangsi (2017) by introducing the important framework of non-opposite multiway cuts. We obtain a substantially improved lower bound of 1.22232 on the approximation ratio of the Multiway Cut problem. Manokaran, Naor, Raghavendra, and Schwartz (2008) showed that under UGC, the approximation ratio of Multiway Cut is equal to the integrality ratio of a simple LP relaxation, known as the CKR relaxation, introduced by Călinescu, Karloff, and Rabani (2000). Thus, stronger LP relaxations are not required for obtaining an optimal approximation algorithm for the problem. We show, however, that relying on the framework of Angelidakis, Makarychev, and Manurangsi (2017), stronger LP relaxations from the Sherali-Adams hierarchy for non-opposite multiway cuts can be used to obtain improved integrality ratios for the CKR relaxation, and hence improved lower bounds on the approximation ratio of the Multiway Cut problem. One of the novel features of our analysis is considering a continuous limit of discrete LPs defined on a simplex. Our proof of the new 1.22232 bound is completely analytic. We also present strong numerical evidence that suggests that our techniques can be used to improve the lower bound to at least 1.23003.

title: SlackBench: Benchmarking Agents on Collaborative Projects Grounded in Real Code Repositories
text: Title: SlackBench: Benchmarking Agents on Collaborative Projects Grounded in Real Code Repositories Mingxuan Li , Huanzhi Mao , Ruitao Zheng , Jarod Stanbury James , Yunze Li , Natanya Anderson , Joseph E. Gonzalez , Alex Dimakis Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Computation and Language (cs.CL) AI Agents are becoming digital coworkers that can browse the web, write code, run experiments, and assist humans over extended horizons. Yet existing benchmarks fall short of real knowledge work: many rely on synthetic data or isolated tasks, missing the complex, multi-party dynamics of collaborative projects, where critical information is scattered across conversations, code, and evolving decisions.
