Our new framework cleanly and extensionally captures existing security definitions, including not only noninterference but also less understood information flow properties that involve downgrading, such as robust declassification and nonmalleable information flow. Past semantics for these properties have relied on intensional downgrading events. Further, we show that all of these properties can be enforced by a practical information-flow type system for a while-language that supports downgrading. Surprisingly, correctness of this type system is also characterized as a real--ideal simulation, with an important implication: the security of heterogeneous, decentralized systems with a strong (real) attacker can be understood by reasoning about a weak (ideal) attacker whose power is restricted to interaction with downgrading. This result explains the usefulness of nonmalleable information flow and related security properties. The results are fully formalized using the Rocq prover and are publicly available.

title: GeoDIVE: Geospatial Descent Informed by Value Estimation
text: Title: GeoDIVE: Geospatial Descent Informed by Value Estimation Hamza Iqbal , Dan Cher , Eric Xing , Pranavi Kolouju , Abby Stylianou , Robert Pless , Nathan Jacobs Comments: Accepted to WACV 2027. Includes supplementary material Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) Finding specific objects, structures, and spatial patterns supports critical work in agriculture, infrastructure planning, environmental monitoring, and disaster response. These features, however, are often dispersed across very large regions and span dramatically different spatial scales, which defines a search space that is costly to embed, maintain, and search naively. We introduce GeoDIVE, a model that treats a multiresolution satellite image gallery as a forest and uses best-first traversal to determine which tiles to encode. At each visited node, a lightweight model then predicts an optimistic estimate of the best query similarity hidden among its descendants using the query and subtree representations. In evaluations with image and open-vocabulary text queries, GeoDIVE matches exhaustive search at 10% of the encoding cost for image queries and leads all tested baselines at every budget in both modalities. To support future evaluation of multiscale geospatial search, we also release object-level image and text queries for Git-10M, constructed from Microsoft building footprints and OpenStreetMap polygons with VLM-generated captions. Source code and models will be made publicly available.

title: Discrete Poincaré and Bogovskii operators for higher order finite element de Rham complexes
text: Title: Discrete Poincaré and Bogovskii operators for higher order finite element de Rham complexes Johnny Guzmán , Pratyush Potu , K. Olav Tyssvang Subjects: Numerical Analysis (math.NA) We present discrete Poincaré and Bogovskii operators for the common finite element discretizations of the de Rham complex of arbitrary polynomial order. We first discuss how such operators arise from a decomposition of the finite element spaces into a lowest order component and a remainder. This results in a fast algorithm for computing grad, curl, and div potentials. We then introduce a nonlocal Poincaré operator on contractible domains, which generalizes existing constructions based on cone operators to arbitrary order by integrating over cones against extended test forms. This requires developing commuting extension operators, which turn out to be related to rational forms. We also show how the nonlocal construction is modified to obtain a discrete Bogovskii operator preserving homogeneous boundary conditions. We further discuss how the ideas of the construction fit into the theory of finite element systems.

title: TACT: A Pragmatic Approach to Qualitative Analysis with an AI Council
text: Title: TACT: A Pragmatic Approach to Qualitative Analysis with an AI Council Rudrajit Choudhuri , Christian Bird , Carmen Badea , Anita Sarma Comments: 12 pages Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC) Qualitative data can tell software teams what their stakeholders need, yet rigorously analyzing thousands of qualitative responses takes expert time that few teams can afford or justify. Teams therefore often face a false choice: leave the responses unanalyzed, or hand them to a large language model and accept its interpretation and judgment. In this paper, we take a pragmatic approach to AI-assisted qualitative analysis and present TACT (Traceable AI Council for Thematic analysis), a procedure that enables such analysis at scale while keeping teams in control of interpretation and judgment. TACT comes in two variants: TACT-Lite, the core AI council procedure, and TACT-Full, which adds adversaries (models from other model families that critique each model's output) and a decision model that surfaces high-uncertainty code assignments. We evaluated TACT on an independent dataset of 256 Stack Overflow threads qualitatively coded by other researchers. Against their labels, TACT's candidate codebook achieved an F1 of 0.75-0.77 and its final coding an F1 of 0.71-0.72. On a held-out sample, agreement between our own manual coding and TACT's coding was Cohen's $\kappa$ of 0.79-0.85. TACT is also economical: model calls cost \$13.77 (TACT-Lite) to \$33.59 (TACT-Full) per 100 threads. Finally, drawing on our experience building and validating TACT, we identify pitfalls in AI-assisted qualitative analysis, describe safeguards to address them, and offer guidance for teams and researchers applying TACT in practice.

title: From Type to Token: Petri Nets, Individual Token Philosophy, and Individualized Causal Effects
text: Title: From Type to Token: Petri Nets, Individual Token Philosophy, and Individualized Causal Effects Fernando Delbianco , Fernando Tohmé , Gustavo Bodanza Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Machine Learning (stat.ML) Structural Causal Models and Bayesian Networks are the dominant framework for representing causal relations. They are fundamentally type-level formalisms since their estimands, Average Treatment Effects and Conditional Average Treatment Effects, are properties of distributions over populations, not of individual units. When treatment effects exhibit unbounded heterogeneity, these estimands collapse. What persists is the structural, token-level core of causation. We argue that Petri Nets under the Individual Token Philosophy are the natural representation of these token-level causal structures. We develop a formal translation from Bayesian Networks to Petri Nets, providing a two-layer account of individualized causality. The PN layer provides a structural representation of causal mechanisms that does not rest on distributional assumptions. In turn, a conformal prediction layer quantifies causal effects with finite-sample coverage guarantees. Together they constitute a complete account of individual causal effects.

title: Memory-Access Profiling for Early Multicore Interference Awareness in Embedded Systems
text: Title: Memory-Access Profiling for Early Multicore Interference Awareness in Embedded Systems Jean-Baptiste Lefoul , Ahmad Shahnejat Bushehri , Alaric Chan Lock , Felipe Gohring de Magalhaes , Gabriela Nicolescu Subjects: Performance (cs.PF) Applications executing on different multicore processors may interfere through shared resources. Such interference can introduce execution-time variability and complicate system integration, especially when applications that behave predictably in isolation are co-scheduled. This paper presents a profiling framework for early multicore interference awareness. The proposed approach captures source-level memory-operation traces from C applications with limited source-code modification and combines them with architectural parameters of the target platform. The framework maps memory accesses to cache sets and memory blocks, generates cache-occupancy profiles and heatmaps, and evaluates pairwise interference risks through a progressive three-stage analysis. First, a coarse-grained screening step classifies applications according to their non-stack memory-access behavior. Second, a static multicore cache-profiling step identifies cache sets whose combined footprint exceeds or approaches the hardware associativity. Third, a temporal footprint analysis tracks intervening unique blocks between consecutive accesses to the same memory block and computes Contention Potential Growth to identify execution windows vulnerable to cache eviction. The framework is evaluated using four benchmark pairings executed on a dual-core platform, with hardware performance counters measuring L2 cache misses used as validation references. The results show that the proposed analysis is consistent with the observed high- and low-risk cases and provides conservative warnings for near-capacity configurations. In particular, different applications pairs might produces up to 213.09% increase in L2 cache misses. These results demonstrate that memory-access profiling can provide practical and interpretable early indicators of cache-related multicore interference before exhaustive hardware testing.

title: Neural networks and games
text: Title: Neural networks and games Philip R. Neary Subjects: Neural and Evolutionary Computing (cs.NE) ; Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Theoretical Economics (econ.TH) Hopfield neural networks and noncooperative games provide seemingly different approaches to understanding how collective outcomes emerge from local interactions. In a neural network, individual units adjust their states according to local signals; in a game, players choose actions to maximise individual payoffs. I establish an exact equivalence between symmetric binary Hopfield networks and binary-action games that admit a quadratic potential. The equivalence identifies stable network configurations with pure-strategy Nash equilibria, and asynchronous neural updating with best-response dynamics. More broadly, the storage and retrieval of memories in neural networks correspond, respectively, to the design and selection of equilibria in games.

title: Agents, Think Only When it Helps
text: Title: Agents, Think Only When it Helps Min-Seon Kim , Seungdong Yoa , Sanghyu Yoon , Ye Seul Sim , Suhee Yoon , Dongmin Kim , Jung-Eun Kim Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG) LLM agent distillation transfers agentic capabilities to student models by training on complete teacher trajectories that typically interleave thoughts and actions. We question how critical thought supervision is for agents' ultimate action performance. To answer this, we disentangle their impacts by independently perturbing teacher thoughts and actions during distillation. On widely adopted agent benchmarks across model scales, altering or discarding thoughts has little effect on student performance. We find, however, that thought supervision becomes important when information about the thought is not disclosed in the corresponding action during training. By identifying such discrepant cases, our findings challenge the common practice of distilling entire teacher trajectories for LLM agents, and offer a new insight that thought supervision can be a discernible choice for efficiency depending on whether the information of thought is disclosed in the action.

title: Self-Supervised Pretraining for Label-Efficient Facial Expression Recognition using Smart Glasses
text: Title: Self-Supervised Pretraining for Label-Efficient Facial Expression Recognition using Smart Glasses Zhengtao Gao , Francesco Bombassei De Bona , Leonardo Alchieri , Ivana Kiprijanovska , Simon Stankoski , Bojan Sofronievski , Hristijan Gjoreski , Marc Langheinrich , Martin Gjoreski Comments: 7 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Best Paper Award at the SEPH 2026 workshop, UbiComp Companion '26 Journal-ref: Companion of the 2026 ACM International Joint Conference on Pervasive and Ubiquitous Computing (UbiComp Companion '26), October 11-15, 2026, Shanghai, China Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) Facial Expression Recognition (FER) on optomyographic (OMG) smart glasses such as OCOsense enables privacy-preserving, camera-free affect sensing for health and well-being. Most FER systems are fully supervised, i.e., they rely either on hand-crafted expert features with classical machine learning, or on end-to-end deep models trained from labelled data. Both depend on large quantities of labelled expressions, which are costly to collect and limit deployment in real-world, personalized settings. We investigate Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) as a route to label-efficient FER on these glasses. We pretrain a Vision Transformer with a masked-autoencoder objective on unlabelled OCOsense recordings and finetune it for five-class FER under person-independent cross-validation. Across label budgets from 5% to 100%, pretraining consistently improves performance; with only 5% of the labels, the pretrained model outperforms the from-scratch model trained with all labels. Our results show that SSL pretraining is a practical way to reduce labelling cost for smart eyewear FER, and we discuss the implications for future personalization and continual adaptation.

title: Reachability Diameter: Beyond the Square-Root Barrier, with Polynomial Hardness
text: Title: Reachability Diameter: Beyond the Square-Root Barrier, with Polynomial Hardness Hector Tierno , Shuang Yang Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS) The reachability diameter of a directed graph is the maximum finite shortest-path distance across all pairs of vertices. It has received recent attention under this name, although the underlying quantity has long played a central role in shortcut set and parallel reachability. Notably, Bals et al. establish hardness for every polynomial-factor approximation in nearly-linear time for weighted digraphs. Yet they give $n^{1/2+o(1)}$-approximation in the unweighted regime with nearly-linear running time, and their conditional lower bounds rule out certain constants only, leaving open whether polynomial loss is necessary. We give a randomized algorithm that estimates the reachability diameter of an unweighted digraph within a factor $n^{1/3+o(1)}$, with high probability, in $\widetilde{O}(m+n)$ time. We complement our algorithm with a lower bound conditional on the 3-uniform Hyperclique hypothesis, ruling out an $n^{2/15-\varepsilon}$-approximation in $\widetilde{O}(m+n)$ time for every fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,2/15)$, establishing the necessity of polynomial loss for nearly-linear time algorithms.

title: Incremental Minimum Spanning Trees on a Napkin
text: Title: Incremental Minimum Spanning Trees on a Napkin Lucian Bicsi , Adrian Budău Comments: 20 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS) In the incremental minimum spanning forest problem, weighted edges arrive one at a time. After each insertion we must report the edge that leaves the minimum spanning forest, and queries ask for the bottleneck distance of two vertices: the smallest possible maximum edge cost on a path between them. Link-cut trees solve both in $O(\log n)$ amortized time. In 2021 we wrote the folklore BottleneckTree, a short competitive-programming structure that stores one parent pointer and one cost per vertex, and conjectured that it also runs in $O(\log n)$ amortized time. We show that this conjecture is false: on a family of inputs, its amortized cost per operation is $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$. We then present a structure with the same state, two arrays and a single loop, and prove that it runs in $O(\log n)$ amortized time per insertion and per query. Unlike the AM-tree of Ding, Gu and Sun, which attains the same bound, it stores no subtree sizes and maintains no balance invariant. For a connected graph with distinct costs, the structure can be viewed as an implicit link-cut tree on the Kruskal reconstruction tree: each rotation corresponds to exactly one preferred-child change, and each skip acts on a stale path-parent pointer. In experiments it is 1.3-2.1 times faster than the folklore BottleneckTree on insertions, up to 480 times faster on its adversarial input, and 6.3-16 times faster than an explicit link-cut tree.

title: CoReFlow: Consistency-Relaxed Flow Maps for Probabilistic Traffic Forecasting
text: Title: CoReFlow: Consistency-Relaxed Flow Maps for Probabilistic Traffic Forecasting Pengnan Chi , Zhiguo Zhang , Xiaoliang Ma Comments: 12 pages, 8 figures Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) Probabilistic traffic forecasting is essential for reliable Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS), as it captures uncertainties in complex road networks. Recent diffusion- and flow-based generative models have facilitated uncertainty modeling through a multi-step sampling process. However, beyond slow inference, this process is designed to capture complex multimodal distributions, which misaligns with the limited complexity of the conditional traffic data distribution, causing models to underperform deterministic baselines. To address this, we introduce the \underline{Co}nsistency-\underline{Re}laxed \underline{Flow} Map (CoReFlow) model, presenting the first effort to leverage the one-step generation capability of flow maps, known as solution operators of probability-flow ordinary differential equations. Besides, we improve accuracy using a concise training objective that supervises the model via interpolation endpoints over finite time intervals. Unlike existing methods (e.g., self-distillation and MeanFlow Identity) that maintain trajectory consistency to model multimodal distributions, our objective leverages conditional mean to restrict the consistency, thereby achieving higher accuracy in the probabilistic traffic forecasting task. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets show CoReFlow achieves state-of-the-art forecasting accuracy. It surpasses recent baselines, provides competitive uncertainty modeling, and reduces inference costs compared to existing generative baselines.

title: How Much Do Modern Embeddings Reveal? Inversion Attacks on Commercial Embedding Models
text: Title: How Much Do Modern Embeddings Reveal? Inversion Attacks on Commercial Embedding Models Kareem Elaasar , Cristina Lopes Comments: 14 pages, 10 tables. Published in BlackboxNLP 2026 Journal-ref: Proc. 9th BlackboxNLP Workshop, pp. 76-89, 2026 Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE) Text embedding inversion reconstructs source text from fixed-dimensional vectors, posing a privacy risk to systems that store embeddings instead of raw text. We adapt the vec2text framework (Morris et al., 2023) to support text-embedding-3-small and mistral-embed alongside GTR-base. We evaluate 800 samples per category across general instructions, Wikipedia passages, paraphrased instructions, health-related instructions, and short literal code snippets, using a common 60-80-character range and paired original and paraphrased instructions. Under the evaluated vec2text configuration, text-embedding-3-small achieves the highest exact-match rate in all five categories, including 47.4% on health-related instructions and 24.5% on general instructions under the evaluation's case-insensitive, whitespace-stripped matching rule. BERTScore F1 exceeds 87 on the 0-100 scale for every prose category and embedder, indicating high contextual similarity to the references. Short code snippets yield lower reconstruction scores. These findings characterize one attack configuration and the selected datasets; they do not establish attack-independent rankings or sensitive-attribute recovery rates. They nevertheless motivate explicit assessment of inversion risk and access controls for stored embeddings.

title: Same Method, Different Task: What the Bitter Lesson Does Not License in Social Simulation
text: Title: Same Method, Different Task: What the Bitter Lesson Does Not License in Social Simulation Justin Downes , Robby Milletich , Newel Hirst Comments: Accepted at the SocialAgent Workshop, NeurIPS 2026 (non-archival). 15 pages, 5 figures Subjects: Multiagent Systems (cs.MA) The bitter lesson holds that general methods leveraging computation defeat hand-encoded domain knowledge. We argue it carries a condition its popular reading omits: in every case Sutton cites, the general method was scaled against the same task the domain engineering was solving. Social simulation substituted across tasks instead, replacing hand-built agents with an artifact optimized for predicting text. The move is bitter-lesson-shaped, but the lesson does not license it. Prediction is a solitary act: the predictor bears no consequences from the interaction it models. Cooperation, defection, and norm enforcement are phenomena of interested parties; they do not exist for a disinterested observer at any scale. What is missing is not emergence, which LLM populations already show, but stakes. We show that several anomalies reported in prior work (excess cooperation that predates alignment training, collective agreement without individual fidelity, and population homogeneity) follow from this account. A 540-agent pilot with pre-specified hypotheses, which tests sensitivity to persistent consequences rather than cooperation, finds that consequences reshape strategies in two of three model families but never produce human-like heterogeneity. We argue for mixed-motive settings that shape agents rather than only test them, and ask whether agents should be pretrained differently from predictors.

title: Cognitive Bias Signatures in Search-Equipped LLM Agents: A Stage-Resolved Analysis
text: Title: Cognitive Bias Signatures in Search-Equipped LLM Agents: A Stage-Resolved Analysis Yanru Xiao , Yingwei Yu Comments: 19 pages, 4 figures Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) Search can help LLM agents correct mistakes, but their starting conditions may shape which evidence they find and use. Drawing on cognitive-bias paradigms, we develop a controlled search harness to examine result order, records of prior work, and initial hypotheses while holding each question and document collection fixed. Matched controls distinguish order effects from differences in document composition and the effects of failed work from context length. Across 10 models and 1,000 synthetic search worlds, we track queries, retrieved documents, document openings, and final answers. Our comparisons suggest that final answers are more sensitive to initial evidence order during active search than when all evidence is supplied in full. Dead-end histories can reduce strategy switching relative to matched neutral histories, indicating an effect beyond context length. Under wrong hypotheses, stage measurements distinguish reduced retrieval or opening from errors that persist after counter-evidence is opened. Exploratory interventions show that opening counter-evidence more often can coincide with lower accuracy, while accuracy can improve with little change in opening.

title: Give the Drafter a Second Chance to Guess: Parallel Reconsideration for Speculative Decoding
text: Title: Give the Drafter a Second Chance to Guess: Parallel Reconsideration for Speculative Decoding Hoang Anh Duy Le , Huibing Dong , Alireza Khadem , Ziteng Sun , Xiang Song , Yizheng Huang , Soroush Radpour , Anshumali Shrivastava , Ye He Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference with a small drafter, whose per-guess acceptance rate determines the achievable speedup. Feature-level drafters share a design choice: every token, easy or hard, is drafted under a single forward pass. Many of the tokens the target rejects are ones the drafter is itself unsure about yet the target answers decisively. To address this, we introduce Parallel Reconsideration: guided by its own uncertainty, the drafter reconsiders its hesitant guesses with extra passes that run in parallel with the one-pass draft, adding negligible latency. A co-designed training recipe and serving-time drafting algorithm append these reconsidered guesses to the original draft tree as refined candidates. Across models and benchmarks, on average, Parallel Reconsideration improves over the baselines by 5.3% to 10.2% on acceptance length and by 3.5% to 9.2% on speedup.

title: Faster Approximate Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances via Near-Optimal Sumset Estimation
text: Title: Faster Approximate Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances via Near-Optimal Sumset Estimation Nick Fischer , Yael Kirkpatrick , Vasileios Nakos Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS) \emph{Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances} is one of the most studied problems in string algorithms: given a text $T$ of length~$n$ and a pattern~$P$, the task is to compute the Hamming distance between~$P$ and every length-$|P|$ substring of~$T$. As exact algorithms have been stuck at time~$\tilde O(n^{3/2})$ for decades, a long line of work has turned to the $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate version of the problem. Milestones include Karloff's $\tilde O(\epsilon^{-2} n)$-time algorithm [IPL '93], followed by randomized improvements to $\tilde O(\epsilon^{-1} n)$ by Kopelowitz and Porat [FOCS '15] and recently to $\tilde O(\epsilon^{-0.915} n)$ by Chan, Jin, Vassilevska W., and Xu [FOCS '23]. In this work, we significantly improve this bound to $\tilde O(\epsilon^{-2/3} n)$, using a considerably simpler algorithm. Our algorithm follows the framework of Chan, Jin, Vassilevska W., and Xu, which reduces the problem to a variant of 3SUM that we call \emph{Sumset Estimation}. We solve Sumset Estimation optimally (up to logarithmic factors) by replacing their matrix multiplication techniques with ideas from sparse recovery. Specifically, we adapt the classic Count Sketch by replacing its random signs with random complex roots of unity---a simple idea that may find further applications for other additive problems. Finally, we give evidence that our running time might in fact be optimal: we show that the $\epsilon^{-2/3}$ dependence is \emph{best possible} for a certain natural class of algorithms, including ours and all previous algorithms.

title: Do Language Models Know Which Constraints Belong Together?
text: Title: Do Language Models Know Which Constraints Belong Together? Junbo Jacob Lian , Kaixuan Chen , Hanzhang Qin , Huiling Chen , Chaoyu Zhang , Chung-Piaw Teo Comments: 23 pages, 4 figures, 15 tables. Code and data: this https URL Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS); Optimization and Control (math.OC) Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation strengthens the linear relaxation of a mixed-integer program by convexifying a chosen set of constraint families, and every candidate costs a column generation run. The choice is hard when families strengthen the bound only together, because a search that adds one family at a time then stops at the linear relaxation. The classical inequalities of lot sizing, network design and facility location rest on such zero-marginal groups. We prove that when each evaluation convexifies at most $s$ of $k$ families, any method that observes only bounds needs a covering number of evaluations, of order $k^w$, to find a hidden group of $w$ families, also on actual Dantzig-Wolfe relaxations. A prediction that misses $e$ members reduces the cost to $\Theta(k^e)$, through one staged search that does not need to know $e$, so the evaluations a prediction saves measure what the predictor knows. We study two sources of predictions. A one-pass lookahead at an optimal LP dual is provably blind to groups whose families share no variable, and a language model reads the names and text of the model. JointDW verifies the prediction of the language model with the staged search and interleaves it with the lookahead at a bounded loss. Groups that strengthen the bound only jointly appear in a quarter of the MIPLIB-NL models whose bound can be improved. There the strongest language models identify them about as often as the lookahead, their predictions rest on the names for textbook models, and reasoning about doubles the accuracy of the same model. On larger models with distracting families, the lookahead finds the group in one evaluation of three families. Language models given only the text seldom name it, while one reasoning model given every coefficient names it in all but one answer and then needs fewer evaluations than the lookahead for pairs of families.

title: RESHPart: Feedback-Reshaped Spectral Embedding for Hypergraph Partitioning
text: Title: RESHPart: Feedback-Reshaped Spectral Embedding for Hypergraph Partitioning Rongjian Liang , Zhuo Feng , Brucek Khailany Comments: Accepted to ASP-DAC 2027 Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC) With scalable Laplacian solvers now available, the next frontier is to exploit them more effectively for high-quality hypergraph partitioning. In this work, we revisit spectral hypergraph partitioning from the perspective of spectral embedding geometry. Through a systematic analysis of circuit hypergraphs and controlled synthetic (hyper)graphs, we identify a ray-like embedding structure that helps explain the effectiveness of projection-based partitioning. We further show that the geometry of spectral embeddings can be systematically influenced through Laplacian design and hyperedge reweighting. Guided by these insights, we propose FRESHPart, a feedback-reshaped spectral partitioning framework that refines the spectral embedding through Geometry Feedback and Search Feedback, producing embeddings that are better aligned with projection-based partitioning. On the Titan23 benchmark, FRESHPart achieves average cut reductions over hMETIS of 13.09% at $\epsilon=2\%$ and 25.21% at $\epsilon=20\%$, surpassing the strongest previously reported results (12.16% and 22.53%, respectively), while completing every benchmark in under 120 s on a single GPU.

title: The Male Abstraction Bias in Internet Culture and Large Language Models
text: Title: The Male Abstraction Bias in Internet Culture and Large Language Models Douglas Guilbeault , Bhargav Srinivasa Desikan Subjects: Computers and Society (cs.CY) ; Computation and Language (cs.CL); Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC) Two foundational aspects of human cognition, abstractness and gender, are typically examined as separable. Here, we find they are systematically linked throughout the entire space of concepts spanning single (N = 40,000) and multi-word expressions (N = 67,000): across billions of words and millions of images on the internet -- and across numerous measurement techniques -- more abstract concepts are more associated with men, an effect which replicates in languages around the world. This pattern not only holds across conceptual domains, but it also maps onto grammatical structure: verbs and adverbs are more abstract and more male-coded, a system-wide trace of stereotypes accentuating agentic qualities in men. Furthermore, this bias emerges in human and AI responses in free association tasks, indicating its internalization and its algorithmic reproduction. The male abstraction bias may underlie and unify a range of stereotypes, evidencing gender as a core organizing dimension in conceptual space.

title: Prospective Memory for Proactive LLM Agents
text: Title: Prospective Memory for Proactive LLM Agents Yuanchen Bei , Zhining Liu , Tianxin Wei , Weizhi Zhang , Zhichen Zeng , Philip S. Yu , Hendrik Hamann , Jingrui He , Hanghang Tong Comments: 17 pages, 8 figures Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) Most memory systems for LLM agents are retrospective, preserving and retrieving past information to inform current decisions. Proactive agents, however, also require prospective memory: retaining future-directed intentions and realizing them when appropriate opportunities arise, even without explicit requests. Crucially, remembering the right intention does not guarantee acting at the right time: a related observation may call for waiting, while a later cue may make the same intention actionable. Inspired by cognitive theories of human prospective memory, we introduce Pro-Memory, a memory framework that separates maintaining future intentions from deciding when and how to realize them. Pro-Memory preserves pending objectives linked to their supporting evidence, assesses new observations against their original goals and activation conditions, and coordinates appropriate contributions with the agent's ongoing actions. It further updates intention states based on actions actually issued or evidence of resolution, while an experience memory distills feedback from completed episodes into guidance for future decisions. Experiments on two benchmarks spanning delayed-intention tasks and open-ended proactive assistance demonstrate consistent improvements in proactive task performance over representative memory approaches across multiple LLM backbones, while limiting unnecessary interventions.

title: Mitigating Spurious Invariance in Contrastive Learning: A Probabilistic Self-Supervised Learning Framework for Medical Image Analysis
text: Title: Mitigating Spurious Invariance in Contrastive Learning: A Probabilistic Self-Supervised Learning Framework for Medical Image Analysis Wei Wei , Yading Yuan Comments: Published in IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging (TMI), 2026. 17 pages Journal-ref: IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging, vol. 45, no. 7, pp. 3862-3877, 2026 Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) Owing to the prohibitive cost of manual annotation for enormous medical images, self-supervised learning (SSL) has gained substantial attention and shown promise in various medical imaging tasks. Among SSL approaches, contrastive learning has emerged as a prominent one, encouraging models to encode semantic information that remains invariant between different augmented views. However, this invariance can be spurious for medical images, as subtle but critical medical features can be suppressed during augmentations. In this paper, we mitigate this issue by encoding the learned feature embeddings as probability distributions rather than fixed vectors, thus capturing a richer and more nuanced spectrum of information. Furthermore, we propose a unified probabilistic framework that seamlessly integrates multiple SSL approaches. Our method achieves superior performance over the state-of-the-art SSL methods on various downstream tasks across multiple datasets, including medical image segmentation and classification. We further validate the method through additional analyses of robustness to stronger augmentations, label efficiency under limited fine-tuning labels, and computational trade-offs. The code is released at this https URL .

title: Self-Supervised Learning of Universal Latent Spaces for Operator Learning
text: Title: Self-Supervised Learning of Universal Latent Spaces for Operator Learning Sepehr Mousavi , Levi Lingsch , Siddhartha Mishra , Laura De Lorenzis Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) Neural operators fit their representation of functions to the task they are trained on, so every new task rebuilds a reduced space from labeled data. Following the self-supervised pre-training that made representations shareable in natural language processing and computer vision, we decouple representation learning from operator learning. A functional autoencoder is pre-trained on analytic functions synthesized on the fly, with no solver and no labels, to represent functions on arbitrary point clouds, and the latent space it induces is frozen and reused across tasks. The representation is exactly equivariant to translation, dilation, and amplitude, and reconstructs solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) and natural images on geometries it never saw. Being task-agnostic, the latent space can be interpreted in its own right. The whole space is used and decodes to valid fields, it preserves the ordering of distances between physical fields, its geodesics interpolate physical evolutions, and edit directions transfer across fields. With frozen representation maps, a dataset is encoded once and a neural operator is trained entirely on cached embeddings, which saves memory and training time. On 28 tasks in fluid dynamics, solid mechanics, acoustics, and the Helmholtz and Poisson equations, this paradigm can exceed the accuracy of state-of-the-art end-to-end architectures, with up to an order of magnitude higher throughput and memory savings that fit models nearly two orders of magnitude larger on consumer-grade GPUs. At inference, latent rollouts run up to an order of magnitude faster than regular rollouts, and chunked inference processes functions of over half a billion points on a single consumer-grade GPU.

title: C-WFDM: A ControlNet-Guided Wavelet-Fusion Diffusion Model for Multimodal Brain MRI Completion
text: Title: C-WFDM: A ControlNet-Guided Wavelet-Fusion Diffusion Model for Multimodal Brain MRI Completion Muhammad Nabi Yasinzai , Remika Mito , Mangor Pedersen Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) Multimodal brain MRI provides complementary anatomical, tissue, and pathological information to support downstream artificial intelligence (AI) applications. However, modality availability is uneven across public and pooled neuroimaging datasets: T1-weighted (T1w) MRI is widely represented, T2-weighted (T2w) and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) MRI are less consistently available, and gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted (T1Gd) MRI is relatively scarce. Pooled datasets therefore contain participants with different combinations of acquired MRI contrasts, reflecting variation in the study designs, acquisition protocols, and clinical or research objectives of the contributing studies. Many missing-modality benchmarks simulate incomplete MRI by withholding contrasts from complete four-modality cases, which may not represent the observed availability patterns in pooled datasets. To address this gap, we introduce C-WFDM, a ControlNet extension of our Wavelet-Fusion Diffusion Model (WFDM), for subject-specific missing-modality completion. C-WFDM is built on an earlier BrainScape snapshot comprising 157 public MRI datasets and 45,880 preprocessed scans. The pretrained WFDM backbone retains target-modality and metadata conditioning, while target-specific ControlNet adapters use MRI contrasts from the same participant to guide synthesis. C-WFDM synthesizes T2w from T1w, FLAIR from T1w and T2w, and T1Gd from T1w, T2w, and FLAIR. Acquired conditioning contrasts are used when available, and generated intermediate contrasts are used only when required. We compare C-WFDM with ALDM, cWDM, and Pix2Pix using paired structural similarity index (SSIM), peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), and mean absolute error (MAE). In the BrainScape completion experiment, C-WFDM achieves the best T2w and FLAIR results among the evaluated models, with SSIM values of 0.9232 and 0.8904, respectively.

title: OdorSpaces: Visual-Olfactory Embodied Navigation in 3D Environments
text: Title: OdorSpaces: Visual-Olfactory Embodied Navigation in 3D Environments Changyeon Lee , Kelin Yu , Zheng Wei , Shuna Ni , Ruohan Gao Comments: Accepted at the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026). 20 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG) Olfaction provides critical information about airborne chemical cues, yet it remains largely underexplored in embodied AI, with limited prior machine olfaction work focusing primarily on semantic odor perception. We introduce OdorSpaces, a physics-based simulation platform and benchmark for visual-olfactory embodied navigation. OdorSpaces augments Habitat-Sim with 3D odor transport and dispersion simulated by Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS), enabling agents to navigate photorealistic indoor environments using both visual and olfactory observations. The benchmark includes two representative source-seeking scenarios: invisible gas-leak localization and early-stage fire localization. We develop an initial multimodal reinforcement learning policy that integrates visual observations and olfactory measurements over time. Experiments show that the policy outperforms a diverse set of baselines, establishing a strong reference for future research on visual-olfactory embodied navigation.

title: PersonaCodeBench: Evaluating Coding Agents in Persona-driven Human-Interactive Sessions
text: Title: PersonaCodeBench: Evaluating Coding Agents in Persona-driven Human-Interactive Sessions Haixin Wang , Jianheng Hou , Hongyu Shen , Wenzhe Fan , Wei-Chieh Huang , Qianyu Zhu , Weichen Li , Taoran Li , Yuhang Yao , Ruohan Wang , Zhejian Peng , Wanting Jiang , Yifan Chen , Shushu Liang , Haoming Li , Defu Cao , Xu Hu , Siyang Wu , Chen Yang , Haodi Hu , Haichao Zhang , Cong Wang , Zhiyuan Yu , Weizhi Zhang , Yifan Wang , Jintao Huang , Yizhou Sun , Yijun Wang , Yuexing Hao , Xiaomin Li Comments: 40 pages, 9 figures Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) Coding agents must deliver correct software while respecting users' expertise, preferences, and working conditions. Existing benchmarks increasingly incorporate interaction, yet personalized requirement fulfillment remains underexplored. We introduce PersonaCodeBench, which turns user characteristics into verifiable obligations in persona-driven multi-turn coding sessions. Our persona pool spans roles, technical abilities, interaction preferences, and practical constraints, yielding task-grounded evolved requirements for implementation, permissions, testing, explanation, and delivery. At runtime, a controller governs user simulator responses and requirement disclosure, using online requirement evaluation to provide feedback and advance the interaction. Requirements emerge progressively, with their content, disclosure conditions, and acceptance criteria fixed before evaluation. A completion verifier and a personalization verifier separately assess native correctness and persona fulfillment. Joint pass requires both adherence to the declared budget and compliance with validity conditions. We evaluate all major frontier agents, establish a comprehensive leaderboard, and conduct detailed experimental analyses to validate effectiveness. PersonaCodeBench supports reproducible evaluation of coding agents' ability to meet explicit, personalized user expectations alongside coding objectives.

title: OUCH: Objective, Uniform, Controlled Haptic Stimulation for Automated Neurological Assessment
text: Title: OUCH: Objective, Uniform, Controlled Haptic Stimulation for Automated Neurological Assessment Sherry Choi , Sitao Sunny Li , Joseph Romero , Lillian Chin , Ashwin G. Ramayya , Allison M. Okamura , Ava Chen Comments: 8 pages, 7 figures. Supplementary video in ancillary files. Sherry Choi and Sitao Sunny Li contributed equally to this work Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) Motor responses evoked by noxious stimulation are used to assess neurological function in hospitalized patients with disorders of consciousness. In standard bedside assessments, these stimuli are applied manually, resulting in substantial variation in force, duration, frequency, and location. Here, we present OUCH (Objective, Uniform, Controlled Haptic stimulation), a wrist-worn device that uses pneumatic actuation to deliver noxious mechanical stimuli. OUCH combines stacked pneumatic pouch actuators, a rigid indenter, and a compliant spacer designed to buckle at a set load, so that the indenter contacts the skin only during actuation. We characterize the device using blocked force tests, clinician evaluation, finite element analysis, and a deformable pressure testbed, and benchmark it against a commercially available handheld pressure algometer. At 200 kPa pouch inflation pressure, our indenter concentrated its load into an estimated contact pressure of 18,500 kPa, over 25 times that of the algometer tip, while requiring less total force. On the deformable testbed, it localized deformation near the surface, while deformation at depth remained comparable to the algometer. As a result, in preliminary perceptual testing, our indenter elicited discomfort at approximately 89% lower applied force than the algometer, demonstrating the feasibility of evoking discomfort with a compact, wearable soft actuator. These results show that combining pneumatic actuation with designed contact geometry enables controlled, repeatable noxious stimulation at the wrist, providing a foundation for objective neurological assessment.

title: Learning Hierarchical Patch Splitting Policies for Faster Vision Transformers
text: Title: Learning Hierarchical Patch Splitting Policies for Faster Vision Transformers Aditya Gupta , Jean Sebastien Dandurand , Kai Qiu , Rohan Choudhury , Laszlo A. Jeni Comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG) Vision Transformers (ViTs) are bottlenecked by the length of their input token sequence. Standard patchification fixes this length with a single patch size applied across the image, regardless of regional content. Prior work on adaptive patch sizing reduces token count by assigning coarser patches to visually simple regions, but relies on noisy pixel-level heuristics such as local entropy to make patchification decisions. We argue that this compute allocation should be grounded in the model's interpretation of task relevant information, not in raw pixel statistics. We introduce Split Policy Learned Image Tokenization which learns to allocate token resolution based on what the model finds meaningful, producing shorter token sequences that are better matched to task-relevant content. SPLIT matches the accuracy of full-resolution ViT classification baselines while using 30% fewer tokens. The same gains hold on dense prediction: SPLIT achieves competitive accuracy on COCO and ADE20K, demonstrating that semantically aligned patchification generalises well beyond classification.

title: Text-Only Domain Adaptation for Low-Resource Medical ASR: Shallow Fusion and Density Ratio Rescoring for Hausa
text: Title: Text-Only Domain Adaptation for Low-Resource Medical ASR: Shallow Fusion and Density Ratio Rescoring for Hausa Oche David Ankeli , Hassan Adelani Luqman , Theodora Ngozi Egbunike , Joshua Gottschalk , Bonaventure F. P. Dossou Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL) Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems often struggle with specialised medical vocabulary, especially in low-resource languages where domain-specific speech data are scarce. We investigate text-only domain adaptation for Hausa medical ASR using the fixed MMS-1B-FL102 acoustic model and two decoding-time language-model fusion methods: Shallow Fusion (SF) and the Density Ratio Approach (DRA). A 4-gram KenLM trained on 19,421 Hausa health sentences serves as the medical target model, while a 75,372-sentence general-domain model provides the source prior for DRA. Evaluation uses 250 recordings of 25 physician-reviewed prompts from 10 speakers across six northern Nigerian states. Under prompt-disjoint five-fold cross-validation, SF and DRA reduce WER from 29.56% to 23.55% and 23.33%, respectively. Both significantly outperform greedy decoding (p < 0.001), while their difference is not significant (p = 0.423). However, general-LM-only SF achieves 23.96% WER, indicating that the medical LM's additional improvement over a general LM is modest. Medical Term Error Rate also improves under fusion, but does not establish a distinct medical-domain advantage. These findings demonstrate that lightweight, text-only language-model fusion can improve Hausa medical ASR without additional domain-specific speech collection.

title: Constraint-Aware Evaluation of Reinforcement Learning and Unsupervised Anomaly Detection for Security Operations Alert Triage
text: Title: Constraint-Aware Evaluation of Reinforcement Learning and Unsupervised Anomaly Detection for Security Operations Alert Triage Radityo Ghifiardi , Rifny Rachman Subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR) Security Operations Centers (SOCs) must identify real threats from large alert streams, but limited analyst capacity means that unnecessary escalations can delay more serious investigations. Existing studies often frame SOC alert triage as classification or anomaly detection, but both views are incomplete for production SOCs, where the central problem is selecting alerts worth escalating under limited capacity, asymmetric error costs, and workload constraints. This paper addresses that gap by formalizing alert triage as a constrained decision problem and evaluating three approaches: an offline reinforcement learning policy trained on alert embeddings, an Isolation Forest model built on operational features, and an autoencoder trained on historical benign alerts. These methods represent different triage assumptions: learning actions from reward, isolating unusual operational patterns, and detecting deviations from benign behavior. We evaluate all methods on 74,909 analyst-labeled production alerts under a strict temporal split and benign-escalation constraint. Because the test set contains 503 unique feature patterns, we primarily rank clusters of similar alerts. At the main operating point, all three methods satisfy the constraint, with the reinforcement learning policy achieving the lowest benign-escalation fraction at 0.000, compared with 0.007 for the autoencoder and 0.041 for Isolation Forest. The methods also prioritize largely different alert clusters, showing complementary rather than redundant coverage. These results suggest that production SOC triage can benefit from constraint-aware evaluation and combined or adaptive deployment of different model families.

title: Energy-Efficient Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Models
text: Title: Energy-Efficient Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Models Rahul Sharma , Nitin Vegesna , Yanxin Zhang Comments: Rahul and Nitin are co-first authors Subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC) Reinforcement learning for language models alternates between generating responses and training the policy. These stages place different demands on GPUs, creating opportunities to reduce clock frequency with little loss in throughput. Selecting frequencies online is difficult because response lengths change and frequency trials themselves consume time and energy. We present EE-RL (energy-efficient RL), an online controller that selects separate frequencies for generation and training during RL execution. It compares candidate settings with a prediction of the default GPU governor on the same token workload, and keeps the most energy-efficient setting that meets a throughput threshold. The controller then monitors throughput and energy and adjusts frequencies as the workload changes. Fixed-frequency sweeps on H100 and GB200 show GPU energy savings of up to 28.2% per valid training token across synchronous and asynchronous execution, while largely preserving throughput. EE-RL turns this headroom into online savings, reducing GPU energy per valid training token by up to 16.9% at a modest throughput cost.

title: Pairing Expert Critique with LLM-Driven Refinement: An Iterative Approach for Curating Quality AI Evaluation Datasets
text: Title: Pairing Expert Critique with LLM-Driven Refinement: An Iterative Approach for Curating Quality AI Evaluation Datasets Honson Ling , Kidus Admassu , Stephanie Rosenthal Comments: 20 pages, 7 figures, 9 tables Subjects: Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG) Evaluating and improving domain-specific LLM responses requires high-quality reference data and rubrics, yet expert authoring is slow and expensive, and synthetic datasets may fail to capture practitioner preferences unless they are grounded in expert judgment. We present SME-C (Subject Matter Expert Critique), a human-AI workflow that captures expertise through lightweight critiques of candidate responses and complements it with LLM-driven analysis and refinement to iteratively curate response datasets and evaluation rubrics. We validate SME-C in the domain of financial business briefs, collecting 3,853 critiques from 411 finance professionals on 520 queries across two survey rounds. We evaluate two LLM-driven refinement strategies: one guided by the experts' written critiques and one that infers critique solely from their preference votes. In a blind validation survey with 100 additional professionals, we found that both strategies significantly improved quality over the experts' top-ranked baseline responses. The gains were concentrated among weaker original responses, and the two strategies excelled in different ways: critique-based refinement produced more domain-grounded improvements, whereas vote-based refinement was more effective at identifying and removing irrelevant content. The resulting rubrics and refined dataset support reproducible offline evaluation and benchmarking of LLMs, suggesting that structured expert critique is a viable alternative to expert authoring for building high-quality, domain-specific evaluation resources more quickly, at scale, and at lower cost.

title: Follow or Surpass? Collaboration, Sound, and the Recognition of Influence in Lineages of Jazz Trumpet Players
text: Title: Follow or Surpass? Collaboration, Sound, and the Recognition of Influence in Lineages of Jazz Trumpet Players Onur Tuncay Bal , Samuel Coavoux , Nathalia A. Loureiro , Balazs Vedres , Mark Wittek Subjects: Social and Information Networks (cs.SI) ; Applications (stat.AP) Cultural fields cohere not only horizontally, through collaboration, but also vertically, through lineages of artistic influence. Considerable attention has been devoted to collaboration networks in various fields of creative production; however, we know less about the structure of artistic influence that is nevertheless key to individual artistic development and the evolution of genres. We examine the structure of such an influence network in a genealogy of 52 prominent jazz trumpet players, combining musicians' discographies, demographic characteristics, geographical locations, and audio analysis of more than 16,000 recordings with exponential random graph models. Direct collaboration, overlap in collaborators, and sonic context similarity, that is, the similarity of the recordings on which players appear, are each associated with an ascribed influence tie, net of the others. Not surprisingly, ascribed ties connect musicians whose recordings share a similar sonic context, but musicians also tend to collaborate with their influences and share collaborators with them. However, players whose recordings share a sonic context and who move in the same circle of collaborators can be thought of as peers or rivals, rather than as influences of each other, because lineage implies a succession predicated on difference as much as on continuity. Taken together, our findings suggest that a field's account of its own evolution is neither a record of who played together nor a map of shared sonic contexts, but a selective ordering that requires both. While our data do not permit a causal account, our aim is to provide a rich and varied methodological strategy and descriptive as well as inferential tools to understand the yet understudied vertical integration of cultural fields through influence ties.

title: Scheduling Data to Compute: Hierarchical Data Pipelining for LLM Training on AMD GPUs
text: Title: Scheduling Data to Compute: Hierarchical Data Pipelining for LLM Training on AMD GPUs Gengyu Rao , Ghadeer Ahmed H Alabandi , Su Ann Chong , Thomas Huber , Kailash Gogineni , Subhajit Dutta Chowdhury , Saleel Kudchadker , Suchita Pati , Zirui Zhang , Zhen Huang , Yanyuan Qin , Xiaoming Peng , Lihuan Zhang , Botao Hu , Wei Huang , Yang Bo , Wen Xie , Xiangyu Zhao , Ruibin Zhang , Xiaobo Chen , Vidushi Goyal , Anshu Raina , Claire Songhyun Lee , Jiakun Yan , Yao Fu , Nusrat Islam , Ravi Dwivedula , Jie Zhang , Maria Garzaran , Zhenyu Gu , Emad Barsoum Subjects: Hardware Architecture (cs.AR) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) Large language models (LLM) have been the key focus of recent machine learning breakthroughs. As the model size grows exponentially, the computation needed for training is astronomical. A GPU can do a huge amount of arithmetic. However, the data its compute units need is not always available when they are ready. This data may still be in slow memory or on another GPU. While the chip waits, expensive compute sits idle, and at scale even a small drop in utilization translates into substantial cost. In this paper, we treat this waiting time as the primary bottleneck. We focus on hardware features designed for explicit data movement. These features load data from off-chip memory onto the chip, rearrange it into the layout the computation requires as it is loaded, and transfer it between GPUs. By orchestrating them, we keep a steady pipeline of data flowing to the compute units so that they remain busy. We present kernel and framework implementations that address this bottleneck using three key data-movement instructions and hardware features. The Tensor Data Mover (TDM) moves tensor data from high-bandwidth memory (HBM) into on-chip memory. Transpose-load instructions transpose tensor data into the layout that LLM computations require as it is loaded on-chip. Finally, System DMA (SDMA) and Remote DMA (RDMA) move data between GPUs over the scale-up and scale-out networks, respectively. Our results show that TDM and transpose-load provide on average 1.88x and 1.19x speedup at the kernel level, respectively. The SDMA and RDMA lead to on average 1.16x and 1.33x speedup for computation overlapped with communication. This is the first AMD LLM training system to utilize all the GPU data pipelining features. Our implementation has been integrated into open source framework and library for AMD GPUs. this https URL this https URL

title: Toward a Compositional Knowledge Architecture for a Shared Organizational Cortex
text: Title: Toward a Compositional Knowledge Architecture for a Shared Organizational Cortex Andrew Miracle , Phyl Georgiou , Christine Okoth , Ese Monday Comments: 25 pages, 10 figures, 10 tables. Evaluation and sources in this https URL (tag registered-plan) Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Information Retrieval (cs.IR) Organizations accumulate evidence in conversations, documents, decisions and relationships, but they act on interpretations: judgements assembled from several observations, resting on assumptions, and revised as circumstances change. Existing retrieval, knowledge graphs and agent memory keep the records and lose the interpretation. We propose a four-layer architecture, Signals, Domains, Claims and Dimensions, in which interpretations persist with their justifications and standing, a truth-maintenance network revises that standing as evidence changes, and validated, versioned Dimensions position interpretations on named axes. We call the result a shared organizational cortex. In a registered retrieval experiment, the Dimension term gains 0.028 nDCG@10 (p = 0.002). In system-level comparisons, the full retrieval configuration improves nDCG@10 by 0.081 over Signals-only and 0.053 over graph-augmented Signals-only retrieval (both reported p < 0.001). The architecture gives organizations a persistent, revisable basis for shared judgement.

title: GRASP: Gradient-Guided Sampling for Contact-Rich Physics-Based Motion Retargeting
text: Title: GRASP: Gradient-Guided Sampling for Contact-Rich Physics-Based Motion Retargeting Yang Liu , Tong Wang , Yiming Bao , Heng Yang Comments: 26 pages, including references and appendices. Project website: this https URL Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) We study physics-based retargeting of human demonstrations for robot learning: finding robot controls that reproduce reference motions under contact dynamics. We propose GRASP (Gradient Recovery from Archived Samples for Proposals), which combines sampling-based exploration with gradient-guided refinement without requiring a differentiable simulator. GRASP-TO extends tempered sequential Monte Carlo by fitting local quadratic cost models to archived rollouts and using their gradients to guide Markov chain Monte Carlo rejuvenation. Metropolis-Hastings correction preserves the target distribution for each fixed proposal kernel, and a population analysis connects the recovered gradients to Gaussian smoothing. GRASP-MPC scales this optimizer to long demonstrations through warm-started receding-horizon planning. Experiments on dexterous hands and humanoids show accurate retargeting with a shared tracking objective and no task-specific contact rewards, including 92.8% success on 1352 bimanual OakInk2 demonstrations. The refined references improve PPO tracking in pen spinning and humanoid-object interaction. We also demonstrate dexterous manipulation and whole-body humanoid motion on real hardware.

title: Decompose the Distillation: Interpretable Single-Pass Guidance for Diffusion Models
text: Title: Decompose the Distillation: Interpretable Single-Pass Guidance for Diffusion Models Wuyang Zhang , Xiaolin Xu Comments: The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Graphics (cs.GR) Classifier-Free Guidance is a widely used inference-time guidance rule for conditional image generation with diffusion models, which exposes a guidance scale that adjusts conditioning strength after training. This flexibility requires conditional and unconditional model evaluations at every sampling step, so an N-step trajectory takes 2N forward passes. Single-pass alternatives reduce such cost, yet most collapse CFG's two components into one opaque guided prediction, losing the separable base flow and guidance direction that support per-step control and diagnostics, even when the scale remains adjustable. This work introduces CtrlFlow, a single-pass guidance method that preserves CFG's separable base-flow and guidance-direction interface. To preserve both components at one-pass cost, CtrlFlow attaches two lightweight LoRA adapters to a frozen backbone, each adding 2.5% parameters, and predicts the base flow and guidance direction from one pass of the shared frozen backbone. Because the guidance scale multiplies the guidance direction only after the forward pass, one evaluation yields the guided velocity at any scale, so a single trained checkpoint remains adjustable at inference without retraining. Preserving two outputs introduces a training mismatch: inference amplifies guidance-direction errors by the chosen scale, while naive component-wise losses weight both outputs equally. To align training with this composed inference-time error, CtrlFlow uses a unified multi-scale distillation loss. Residual guidance errors can still persist at extreme scales, where even small guidance-direction errors are amplified by the guidance scale. To reduce this inference-time error, CtrlFlow applies scale-adaptive modulation to damp velocity-field errors and time-grid warping to concentrate solver evaluations where the trajectory changes most rapidly.

title: Flow-Optimal Separators for Minor-Free and Induced-Minor-Free Graphs in Linear Time via Follow the Regularized Leader
text: Title: Flow-Optimal Separators for Minor-Free and Induced-Minor-Free Graphs in Linear Time via Follow the Regularized Leader Hung Le , Jack Spalding-Jamieson Comments: 34 pages, 4 figures Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS) We give a new algorithm for finding balanced separators in minor-free and induced-minor-free graphs. A key technical idea is a new connection to online learning: we formulate a continuous, non-convex optimization problem and solve it using the Follow the Regularized Leader (FTRL) framework. Our implementation of each FTRL step yields a purely combinatorial algorithm that assigns and adjusts vertex weights over multiple rounds. For graphs with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, we obtain the following results. (1) For $H$-induced-minor-free graphs, we find a balanced separator of size $O(\log(|V(H)|)\sqrt{|V(H)|+|E(H)|}\sqrt{m})$ in expected linear time for fixed $H$. As a corollary, we find balanced separators of size $O(\sqrt{m})$ in string graphs in expected linear time, without requiring string representations. (2) For $K_h$-minor-free graphs, we find a balanced separator of size $O(h\log h\sqrt{n})$ in expected linear time for fixed $h$. Our algorithm unifies two long lines of work on separators in minor-free graphs, dating back to Alon, Seymour, and Thomas (1990): one optimizing separator size and the other optimizing running time. It also gives a natural interpretation of the vertex weighting scheme in a recent linear-time algorithm by Bonnet, Korhonen, Le, Li, and Masarik (2026). The separator bounds for both graph classes are flow-optimal: techniques based on flow-cut duality, including ours, cannot yield balanced separators of asymptotically smaller size.

title: Mechanical Engineering Skills: An Open Library of Agent Skills for Design, Analysis and Manufacturing
text: Title: Mechanical Engineering Skills: An Open Library of Agent Skills for Design, Analysis and Manufacturing Achuth Chandrasekhar , Jesse Barkley , Peter Pak , Rumi Loghmani , Aakash Oza , Amir Barati Farimani Subjects: Multiagent Systems (cs.MA) Mechanical engineers use specialized tools for CAD, simulation, manufacturing and research, each with a distinct interface and learning curve. We present Mechanical Engineering Skills, an open library of 33 agent skills that makes these capabilities accessible through a single text or voice conversation. Each skill combines operating instructions, executable tools and verification procedures. A language model interprets the request, selects and coordinates skills, while deterministic tools perform computations and return checked results. Default workflows require no tool-specific interface training, local model execution or model fine-tuning; skills load on demand and install with one command. Nineteen skills adapt published or preprint research from our laboratory, including text-to-CAD, linkage synthesis, CFD setup, stress-field and lattice surrogates, equation discovery, additive-manufacturing planning and in-process monitoring. Fourteen additional skills support core engineering and education. We describe the skill format, design principles and a method for translating research into practical workflows. Five case studies with explicit evidence scopes and independent reruns demonstrate exact analytical agreement for lattice homogenization, rocket apogee predictions within 4% of stored OpenRocket references, an equation fit nine times more accurate than a cubic polynomial at an unseen temperature, and an end-to-end rehearsal of porosity monitoring. Controlled agent comparisons remain future work. The open library is available at this https URL .

title: PAYWORTHY: Can LLMs Predict Which Freelance Jobs an AI Agent Will Complete?
text: Title: PAYWORTHY: Can LLMs Predict Which Freelance Jobs an AI Agent Will Complete? Mohammad Reza Rezaei , Dingxian Wang , Brett Levert , Celeste Fejzo , Andrew Rabinovich , Zhao Chen Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Computation and Language (cs.CL) Before an AI agent takes on a paid job, someone has to judge whether it is likely to succeed. We test whether frontier language models can make this call before any attempt. We propose PAYWORTHY which contains 1{,}494 real freelance job postings, sampled from 18.8M postings made between 2020 and 2026 on a freelancing platform. An agent attempts each job from the posting alone in a single run, and an LLM judge acting as the client decides whether to accept the work. We ask 18 models to forecast how likely the agent is to succeed and measure how well each model's forecasts rank the accepted jobs above the rejected ones (AUC, where 0.5 is a random ranking). The answer depends on how the agent is described. Told what the agent cannot do, every model ranks the jobs well (AUC 0.66--0.86). Told instead that it is a generic agent with a browser and code execution, the same models rank the same jobs about as well as a random ordering (0.45--0.56). These results hold under judges from four other model families (Claude, GLM, Kimi and Qwen), and the informed forecasts also rank the verdicts of two human raters. Code is available at this https URL

title: BobFlow: Towards Human-Agent Collaborative Data Science Using Dataflows
text: Title: BobFlow: Towards Human-Agent Collaborative Data Science Using Dataflows Jiadong Bai , Yicong Huang , Chen Li Subjects: Databases (cs.DB) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC) Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have established human-agent collaboration as a promising paradigm for data science. Effective collaboration requires a shared computational abstraction that enables agents to reason about processing logic while allowing human analysts to understand, guide, and refine the analysis. Although scripts written in Python or SQL provide precise control, their syntax and execution details can be difficult for analysts to understand and modify. In this paper, we argue that dataflows are an effective abstraction for human-agent collaboration in data science. We introduce BobFlow, a system that combines the dataflow abstraction with the ReAct paradigm. It enables agents to iteratively construct and execute dataflows for data science tasks while allowing analysts to inspect the analysis and provide feedback. Our user study shows that BobFlow helps analysts understand, inspect, and verify agent-generated analyses. A thorough experimental evaluation across proprietary and open-weight LLMs shows accuracy score gains of up to 18.6 points at just over 1/3 of a script-based ReAct agent's inference cost.

title: Classifying K-Geodetic Graphs Via Combinatorial Designs and Distance-regularity
text: Title: Classifying K-Geodetic Graphs Via Combinatorial Designs and Distance-regularity Carlos E. Frasser Comments: 46 pages, 4 figures Subjects: Discrete Mathematics (cs.DM) The classification of K-geodetic graphs is a fundamental problem in graph theory concerning the number of shortest paths connecting pairs of vertices. A graph is called K-geodetic if every pair of distinct vertices is joined by at most K geodesics, where a geodesic is a shortest path between two vertices. The cases K=1,2,3 correspond, respectively, to geodetic, bigeodetic, and trigeodetic graphs. Despite substantial progress in the study of their structural properties, a comprehensive classification of these graph families remains elusive. This paper develops a research framework for investigating the classification problems by combining metric graph theory, distance-regular graphs, algebraic graph theory, and combinatorial design theory. Particular attention is given to distance-regular graphs, for which the number of geodesics between vertices at a fixed distance is determined by the intersection numbers of the graph. This property converts the K-geodetic condition into a finite collection of arithmetic inequalities. We establish the resulting necessary conditions for K=1,2,3, discuss representative examples, and distinguish these conditions from the stronger requirements needed to prove the existence and classification of graphs with a given intersection array. The paper also investigates the potential role of balanced incomplete block designs (BIBDs) in constructing and organizing families of K-geodetic graphs. Finally, it proposes a computational research methodology based on constraint satisfaction, graph-isomorphism testing, exhaustive enumeration, and machine-assisted conjecture generation.

title: ME^2FDiff: Multiscale Expert Enhancing Feature Diffusion in Residual Network for Brain Tumor Segmentation
text: Title: ME^2FDiff: Multiscale Expert Enhancing Feature Diffusion in Residual Network for Brain Tumor Segmentation Afrida Rahman , Bijoy Kundu Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) Automated segmentation of post-treatment glioma from MRI is essential for accurate diagnosis and treatment planning, yet remains difficult. Surgery and chemoradiotherapy cause structural changes in brain like resection cavities, edema, and fibrosis, that alter imaging appearance and mimic tumor recurrence. Contemporary segmentation architectures attain high accuracy with two limitations. First, the bottleneck originates from the deepest encoder stage, so one representation must serve sub-regions that differ widely in size and appearance. Second, they produce the segmentation in a single forward pass with no mechanism for refinement. We propose ME^2FDiff, a single-model architecture, addressing both. An attention-conditioned spectral diffusion block refines the bottleneck. It uses the image-conditioned latent diffusion process with two processes: a spatial pre-attention gate and a spectral fusion block whose timestep-adaptive bandpass filter selects the informative frequency band at each noise level. A multiscale expert-enhanced feature block fuses the intermediate encoder scales into the bottleneck through expert-selected shared tokens, guaranteeing balanced utilization without an auxiliary loss. On the BraTS 2024 post-treatment glioma dataset, ME^2FDiff achieves the best results on every tumor sub-region among all single-model baselines (91.23% Dice, 84.52% IOU, 2.13 mm HD95 on whole-tumor) and surpasses a three-expert ensemble on both overlap metrics at roughly one-third of its inference cost. Against recent state-of-the-art methods retrained under identical conditions, it maintains the strongest performance with the fewest parameters of any competing model. These findings demonstrate that a single, compact network can absorb the specialization, usually sought through ensembling or larger architectures.

title: Noncrossing is All You Need: Beyond Identical Delay Functions in Online Matching with Delays on General Metrics
text: Title: Noncrossing is All You Need: Beyond Identical Delay Functions in Online Matching with Delays on General Metrics Yossi Azar , Junhao Gan , Shahar Lewkowicz , Xiao Sun , Seeun William Umboh Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS) Online optimization with delays has emerged as a powerful paradigm with numerous applica- tions, including matching, caching, server management, network design, and set cover. In most of these problems, competitive algorithms are known for arbitrary monotone delay functions, even when different requests are associated with different delay functions. The notable exception is online matching with delays, where all previously known algorithms achieving constant or polylogarithmic competitive ratios require the delay functions to be identical, either linear or concave, and known in advance. We study the online minimum-cost perfect matching with delays problem on general metrics. We introduce the broad class of noncrossing delay functions, which strictly generalizes the classic setting of identical concave delay functions while naturally modeling scenarios in which different requests may experience different delay costs. We present the first deterministic $O(1)$-competitive algorithm for the single-location online matching problem with noncrossing delay functions in the non-clairvoyant setting as well as a randomized $O(lognlog\Delta+log^2\Delta)$-competitive algorithm of an arbitrary metric space where $n$ is the number of points of the metric space and $\Delta$ is its aspect ratio. Our result allows each request to have an arbitrary noncrossing delay function, thereby simultaneously removing the assumptions of identical delay functions, concavity, and clairvoyance that were required by all previous constant or polylogarithmic-competitive algorithms.

title: How Well Can Large Language Models Impersonate Individual Authors? A Comparative Evaluation
text: Title: How Well Can Large Language Models Impersonate Individual Authors? A Comparative Evaluation Harshit Gupta , Shunichi Ishihara Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) This study investigates the authorship impersonation capacity of six widely used large language models (LLMs): Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Opus, GPT 5.2, GPT 5.2 Pro, DeepSeek 3.2, and Grok 4.1 Fast. The evaluation was conducted using short product review texts selected to ensure high within author consistency in individual writing style. Two types of in context prompt were designed: a simple prompt with minimal instruction and a complex prompt incorporating explicit stylometric guidance for mimicry. Authorship mimicry was evaluated using a cosine distance based distance to training metric, supplemented by visual analyses of embedding distributions. The results indicate that authorship impersonation remained challenging for most LLMs, with Gemini 3 Pro showing the strongest apparent mimicry performance. However, subsequent overlap analysis revealed that Gemini 3 Pro extensively copied and reused sentences and phrases from the training texts, at levels far exceeding those observed among human authors. Follow up factor analyses showed that training set consistency was the most robust predictor of mimicry success across models, whereas author distinctiveness did not generalise as a reliable predictor. Global embedding visualisations further revealed a consistent macro level pattern: for most models, generated texts occupied regions of the embedding space that were largely separated from the corresponding human training clusters. This indicates limited convergence towards target author style and suggests the presence of model specific lexical and phraseological preferences. The findings highlight the importance of distinguishing genuine stylistic imitation from direct textual reuse and have implications for the forensic analysis of textual evidence involving potential LLM enabled impersonation.

title: Hotplug Coded Caching: Embedding the YMA and Interference Elimination Schemes via Reed--Muller Codes
text: Title: Hotplug Coded Caching: Embedding the YMA and Interference Elimination Schemes via Reed--Muller Codes Daniela Tuninetti Comments: companion paper to arXiv:2611.03045 Subjects: Information Theory (cs.IT) ; Signal Processing (eess.SP) In the hotplug coded caching model, $K$ users fill their caches of size $M$ as a function of $N$ files, but only an unknown subset of $A<K$ users is active in the delivery phase. We recently showed that (i) under uncoded placement, offline users cause a strict load penalty at intermediate memory sizes, so that coded placement is needed; and (ii) for $AM\leq N$, every classical scheme with row-wise placement, including the scheme of Gomez-Vilardebo (GV), can be embedded in a Reed-Solomon code, which removes the penalty. In this note, we show that every point of the scheme of Yu, Maddah-Ali and Avestimehr (YMA) for a classical system with $A$ users is achievable in the hotplug model for every $K\geq A$. Each user is associated with a hyperplane and each file with a homogeneous polynomial; each user caches the restriction of the polynomial to its hyperplane, and the subfiles seen by the active users are the values of the polynomial at the points where their hyperplanes meet.
