Acting on it requires knowing which inputs are solvable, so information, not the policy, drives the gain. With a verifier and a prior from a related model's past runs on the same inputs, Thompson Sampling raises the solved share on the hardest workload from 14% to 27%; without such a prior, no policy we tested beats round-robin. For the policies we tested, the gain vanishes between prior rank correlations of about 0.3 and 0.55, which cheap text-based priors barely reach on the weakest models, and it requires a verifier whose false acceptances are rare relative to the pass rate. On new Qwen2.5 samples the pattern holds, and tempering the prior avoids losses on easy workloads. We turn these results into a decision guide.

title: Reassessing Dataset Quality and Fine-Tuning Practices for Vulnerability Detection on PrimeVul dataset
text: Title: Reassessing Dataset Quality and Fine-Tuning Practices for Vulnerability Detection on PrimeVul dataset Norbert Sándor Szolnoki , Gábor Antal Comments: Presented at EASE 2026 AI Models/Data track: this https URL Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE) Recent studies report promising results from supervised fine-tuning of pre-trained code language models for automated vulnerability detection on benchmarks such as PrimeVul. In this paper, we present a large-scale empirical evaluation of both model performance and dataset quality in this setting. We systematically fine-tune three widely used encoder models (CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, and UniXCoder) across five imbalance mitigation strategies, extensive hyperparameter sweeps, and multiple random seeds, resulting in 770 independent training runs. Our results reveal a consistent pattern. While standard metrics such as F1 and ROC-AUC occasionally suggest improvements, security-critical and calibration-aware measures tell a different story. Matthews Correlation Coefficient remains near zero, predicted probabilities are poorly calibrated, and evaluation under strict false-positive constraints reveals high false-negative rates. Neither imbalance handling, threshold optimization, nor post-hoc calibration recovers a meaningful discriminative signal. We also conduct a data quality assessment of the PrimeVul benchmark and identify structural issues such as minimal semantic differences between vulnerable and fixed functions, and annotation noise introduced by commit-level labeling. These findings suggests that the PrimeVul dataset, in its current form, presents significant challenges for reliable AI-based vulnerability detection in software engineering with the methodologies we used. Our study highlights the need for more robust dataset design, improved evaluation protocols, and rethinking of fine-tuning practices for security-critical tasks.

title: Corralling AI Risks with Grassroots Contracts
text: Title: Corralling AI Risks with Grassroots Contracts Ehud Shapiro Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Computation and Language (cs.CL); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA) AI's inflection point is a fountain of alarming risks. Digital platforms in particular are vulnerable to three major AI risks, as those in control of global platforms cede control to AI, of the algorithms, of membership and of content: (1) AI control of global platforms, social and economic, used by the majority of humanity, resulting in the majority of humanity becoming vulnerable to AI control. (2) Unaccountable AI agents operating anonymously on social and economic digital platforms, side-by-side with humans, possibly masquerading as humans, serving unknown masters with unknown goals, operating under unknown restraints without accountability or culpability. (3) Unattributed deepfakes generated by anonymous AI, with people unable to distinguish them from genuine content and with their producers evading accountability and culpability. Here, we propose to corral these AI risks with grassroots contracts, a digital incarnation of a two-centuries old notion of Pierre-Joseph Proudhon. We present grassroots contracts for a social graph with accountable AI agents and for a social network with digital provenance, and working smartphone apps that implement the two and show how they corral these major AI risks: (1) AI control of global platforms. (2) Unaccountable AI agents. (3) Unattributed deepfakes.

title: NanoKV: High-Ratio KV Cache Compression for Autoregressive Video Generation
text: Title: NanoKV: High-Ratio KV Cache Compression for Autoregressive Video Generation Jiacheng Lu , Haoyi Zhu , Sipei Yi , Enze Xie , Cheng Zhuo , Yu Li Comments: 25 pages, 13 figures. Project page: this https URL . Code: this https URL Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) Autoregressive video models rely on historical key-value (KV) caches to preserve scene consistency over extended rollouts, making KV storage and repeated attention over history a growing memory and computational bottleneck. Aggressive compression can degrade generation quality, while reconstructing full-dimensional KV leaves attention computation largely unchanged. We introduce NanoKV, a frozen-backbone framework for generation-aware high-ratio KV compression. NanoKV exploits redundancy across tokens and attention heads by storing shared content in cluster centers and encoding joint head-channel residuals into low-bit coefficients. Crucially, NanoKV uses different fitting objectives for Keys and Values according to their distinct roles in attention: Key decoders are optimized to preserve downstream block outputs, whereas Value encoders and decoders are fitted for faithful reconstruction through the deployed quantization path. Building on the same compressed representation, the optional NanoKV-Fast variant reuses the stored coefficients for mixed-dimensional attention, reducing computation without modifying the video backbone. Across three autoregressive video backbones, NanoKV consistently improves the quality-storage trade-off. On HY-WorldPlay, NanoKV achieves $26.09\times$ effective KV compression, nearly twice that of KVTC, while improving PSNR by 1.0 dB. NanoKV-Fast retains $20.53\times$ effective compression and achieves an approximately $1.15\times$ end-to-end speedup over KVTC.

title: UniLoop: Unified Loop Closure Detection from Retrieval to Geometric Verification and Relative Pose Estimation
text: Title: UniLoop: Unified Loop Closure Detection from Retrieval to Geometric Verification and Relative Pose Estimation Jingwen Yu , Pengyu Wang , Jin Wu , Weinan Chen , Ping Tan , Hong Zhang Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) Loop closure detection conventionally cascades separate models for global retrieval, geometric verification, and relative pose estimation, leading to redundant computation and disconnected visual representations. We propose UniLoop, a unified framework that reuses the hierarchical representations of the pretrained geometric foundation model throughout this pipeline. A shared image encoder produces features for compact global descriptors; the same features are passed to the cross-view decoder for pairwise verification; and the original geometric predictions provide relative camera constraints for pose-graph optimization. Experiments on place recognition, loop verification, and relative pose estimation show that UniLoop improves loop-closure robustness and accuracy while reducing redundant backbone computation relative to modular pipelines. UniLoop achieves the best Recall@10 on MSLS (96.6) and Pitts30k (99.3) among the compared methods, while its verification branch reaches 95.63 AP and 96.29 ROC-AUC, surpassing the existing geometric verification baselines.

title: Does Context Compression Preserve Refusal Alignment?
text: Title: Does Context Compression Preserve Refusal Alignment? Anthony Nguyen , Wenjun Lin Comments: Presented at Canadian AI 2026 Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Computation and Language (cs.CL) Context compression reduces inference cost by encoding inputs into compact representations while preserving semantic content. An open question is whether semantic preservation alone is sufficient to maintain downstream behaviours such as refusal alignment. We investigate this question and find that encoder-based compression systematically weakens refusal behaviour in instruction-tuned language models, despite high reconstruction fidelity. This effect persists across model families and compression architectures. Mechanistic analysis shows that compression attenuates activation along the decoder's learned refusal direction. We further explore Memory Steering, a lightweight inference-time intervention that restores refusal rates to near-baseline levels without retraining and operates entirely in compressed representation space. These results demonstrate that semantic preservation does not guarantee behavioural preservation under compression, highlighting the need to explicitly preserve alignment-relevant features in compression-aware systems.

title: LegalEvolver: Agentic Legal Judgment Prediction via Rubric-Guided Self-Evolution
text: Title: LegalEvolver: Agentic Legal Judgment Prediction via Rubric-Guided Self-Evolution Xinyu Yang , Jiejun Tan , Chenlong Deng , Chenghao Zhang , Tongyu Wen , Zhicheng Dou Comments: 20 pages, 5 figures Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Computation and Language (cs.CL) As LLM-based agents develop, they have been increasingly applied in the legal domain. Legal Judgment Prediction~(LJP) requires models to conduct multi-step reasoning and external legal evidence retrieval. Existing legal search agents' performance is often constrained by the quality of retrieval queries. They often formulate queries directly from the initial user request, overlooking latent legal issues and legally salient details. To address this issue, we propose \emph{LegalEvolver}, a query optimization framework specifically designed to generate legally informative queries for LJP-oriented retrieval. Sampling high-quality optimized queries and their corresponding search trajectories is challenging, as relying solely on unguided high-temperature rollouts is both inefficient and constrained by the model's initial capabilities. We therefore heuristically optimize queries as seeds, improving the efficiency of trajectory generation. Furthermore, we summarize rollout experience into rubrics and use them to guide multi-round iterative self-evolution. Iteratively performing rubric optimization and rubric-guided RL enables the model to surpass its initial performance ceiling. End-to-end performance on extensive benchmarks demonstrates the effectiveness of query optimization on LJP. Comparisons with direct SFT followed by RL demonstrate the effectiveness of rubric guidance. Evolving rubrics further outperform fixed rubrics, confirming the benefits of self-evolution.

title: From hydrological laws to catchment models: A process-based model matches deep-learning accuracy on three continents
text: Title: From hydrological laws to catchment models: A process-based model matches deep-learning accuracy on three continents Xilin Xia Comments: 61 pages, 12 figures, 13 tables, plus 19 pages of Supporting Information Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Dynamical Systems (math.DS); Geophysics (physics.geo-ph) Dooge asked whether hydrology has laws at the catchment scale. We ask whether a low-dimensional system built under physical laws can match the accuracy of neural networks that outperform process-based models on the same inputs. Three laws constrain a lumped catchment model. Conservation makes it a flux-connected storage network, dissipation fixes the sign of every flux and aggregation determines how the unresolved composition enters the fluxes, through effective laws over threshold distributions and a memory of the forcing. These laws admit four kinds of refinement. A parsimonious model under them, CaRT (11 parameters per catchment), is refined in a loop assisted by AI agents. Each refinement addresses an observed deficit through a hypothesis from the literature. The result, CaRT+, has fourteen states, 35 parameters per catchment and no daily neural network. Most refinements follow from aggregation over thresholds or from variables that carry no water but modulate fluxes. On 602 British and 593 US gauged catchments, single CaRT+ models reach median Nash-Sutcliffe efficiencies of 0.863 and 0.765 in held-out years. A stateful LSTM reaches 0.869 and 0.751 and an entity-aware LSTM 0.862 and 0.754, while three-seed LSTM ensembles remain ahead of the CaRT+ ensemble by 0.003-0.012 in median paired NSE. On 505 drier Australian gauged catchments unused in development, single CaRT+ models reach 0.778 against 0.762 and 0.753 for the two LSTMs. The results suggest that catchment-scale laws exist as laws of form, with the constitutive families shared and only their parameters learned.

title: Presentation Sensitivity in Typed Decision Models for Subjective Text Evaluation
text: Title: Presentation Sensitivity in Typed Decision Models for Subjective Text Evaluation Jatin Agrawal , Radhika Mamidi Comments: 27 pages, 1 figure, includes appendices Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) Typed decision models offer structured choices, scores, and probabilities for low-cost automated evaluation. We present a controlled audit of presentation sensitivity in Jev, Clef Flash, and Perplexity Decider across native choice and score interfaces. Across six datasets with 9,000 multiply annotated humor, helpfulness, and summarization items, we collect 702,000 judgments under interventions that vary positions, identifiers, authorship claims, endorsements, decision framing, and rating rubrics while preserving the evaluated texts. Jev's second-position probability advantage reaches 6.11 percentage points on summaries; reversing reader endorsements changes Perplexity's selected humor text on 40.40% of pairs; and rejection framing reduces Clef's summary agreement with human preferences by 23.36 points. Rating formats also shift score levels while often preserving rankings. Across these findings, repeatability, presentation robustness, and human alignment emerge as distinct properties of an evaluator. Reliable use therefore requires validating the decisions and score interpretations on which an evaluation pipeline depends.

title: Spatial Differences Analysis of Nodal Frequency Considering Frequency-Voltage Coupling
text: Title: Spatial Differences Analysis of Nodal Frequency Considering Frequency-Voltage Coupling Xiaodan Li , Donghai Zhu , Zining Liu , Zhu Guo , Jiabing Hu , Hong Rao Subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY) The rising penetration of inverter-based resources (IBRs) brings rich control dynamics that can amplify spatial differences in nodal frequency through frequency-voltage (F-V) coupling. Existing analyses often neglect voltage dynamics or only examine the aggregate frequency, leading to overoptimistic evaluation of frequency security. To address these drawbacks, this paper develops a unified model of synchronous generators (SGs), grid-following (GFL)-IBRs, and grid-forming (GFM)-IBRs based on the magnitude and phase dynamics of equivalent internal electromotive force (EMF). Integrating these source models with network equations yields a sparse implicit closed-loop model, which fully captures the device-network F-V coupling without transfer-matrix inversion. Then, the obtained nodal responses are decomposed into common and differential modes. Using this decomposition, coupling indices and pole-residue analysis reveal how F-V coupling can amplify spatial differences in nodal frequency and how source configuration and parameters modify this effect. Finally, case studies on the modified IEEE 39-bus and 118-bus test systems validate the proposed model and demonstrate its computational efficiency.

title: Shoot on (Core)Sight: Re-enabling Secure Debug on the RP2350 with Photon-Emission Microscopy and Laser Fault Injection
text: Title: Shoot on (Core)Sight: Re-enabling Secure Debug on the RP2350 with Photon-Emission Microscopy and Laser Fault Injection Antoine Plin Comments: pre-print Subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR) Fault-resistant policy storage does not guarantee fault-resistant enforcement. We demonstrated this distinction on the RP2350A4 using differential photon-emission microscopy (PEM) and laser fault injection (LFI). PEM narrowed the area for laser scanning, which found two sites where pulses set the DEBUGEN bits enabling core~1 Secure debug. An online attack sequence using only Serial Wire Debug (SWD) feedback restored sustained access. After rescue reset, the sequence recovered a 128-bit test secret. This reset reloads the secret's runtime page lock from a stored policy that permits Secure reads and prevents user firmware from tightening the lock.

title: Partially Dynamic Algorithms for Single-Source Temporal Paths
text: Title: Partially Dynamic Algorithms for Single-Source Temporal Paths Davide Bilò , Bartłomiej Bosek , Jadwiga Czyżewska , Evangelos Kipouridis , Karol Węgrzycki , Anna Zych-Pawlewicz Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS) We present efficient partially dynamic algorithms for maintaining earliest arrival times from a fixed source in temporal digraphs with $n$ vertices. For the incremental scenario where updates are arc insertions, our algorithm has a constant query time and requires a total update time of $O(n + m \log m)$, where $m$ is the total number of arcs added to the arc-less graph. For the decremental scenario where updates are arc removals, our algorithm has a constant query time and requires a total update time of $O(n + m \log m)$, where $m$ is the number of arcs in the graph upon its initialization. We also consider earliest-arrival queries with an arbitrary departure-time threshold and develop an incremental algorithm with $O(n+\Delta_s m\log m)$ total update time, $O(\log m)$ query time, and $O(n+m)$ space, where $\Delta_s$ is the number of distinct departure times of arcs leaving the source. All of our algorithms are also capable of reporting an earliest arrival path from the source to the queried vertex $v$ in constant time per edge once the earliest arrival time at $v$ is known. We complement our positive results with conditional lower bounds based on the Online Boolean Matrix-Vector Multiplication conjecture (a.k.a. OMv conjecture). For both the incremental and the decremental scenarios, we show the non-existence of an algorithm with $O(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ amortized update time and $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ amortized query time, even if the algorithm is randomized and latencies on the arcs are uniform. For arbitrary departure-time queries, we also establish an OMv-based conditional lower bound showing that our incremental algorithm is optimal up to logarithmic factors on dense temporal graphs. Thus, efficient total running time is essentially the best outcome we can get. Our conditional lower bounds hold also for the case of undirected temporal graphs.

title: MA-Mesh: Resilient Multi-Agent Collaboration via Role-based Self-Healing
text: Title: MA-Mesh: Resilient Multi-Agent Collaboration via Role-based Self-Healing JunYong Lee , Woo Kyung Kim , Honguk Woo Comments: Accepted at EMNLP 2026 (Main) Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) Effective collaboration in multi-agent systems requires mechanisms for coordination and adaptability in dynamic and uncertain environments. However, existing multi-agent systems rarely model resilience explicitly, instead relying on ad-hoc output correction that limits systematic, runtime management of robustness. In this work, we propose Multi-Agent Mesh (MA-Mesh), a framework that constructs a role-based self-healing layer on top of a collaboration pattern. Specifically, MA-Mesh generates resilience-aware system specifications and synthesizes them into executable multi-agent policy code. To enhance resilience, we introduce two self-healing mechanisms: Cross-agent reflection, a mechanism that allows agents to evaluate not only their own outcomes but also the performance of their peers, enabling informed behavioral adjustments and collective policy refinement; Role-based failover, a strategy which dynamically reassigns roles and enables agents to substitute for one another when sub-tasks fail or agents underperform, ensuring continuity of task execution. Experimental results across diverse tasks (e.g., software development, tool use, scientific reasoning) demonstrate that MA-Mesh significantly outperforms existing multi-agent systems in both task performance and robustness under system uncertainty.

title: KolTa: A Physics-Informed Active Learning Framework for Formulation Discovery with Limited Data
text: Title: KolTa: A Physics-Informed Active Learning Framework for Formulation Discovery with Limited Data Boyong Tang , Tao Wang , Lei Yang Comments: 21 pages, including 11 pages of supplementary material; 4 figures Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) Finding high-performing formulations is difficult when few have been measured and experimental budgets are limited. We propose KolTa, an active learning framework that selects batches to discover the top 5% of formulations at a target temperature under a fixed query budget. KolTa combines a three-stage predictor of component contributions, role-conditioned interactions, and anchored temperature response with task-specific soft physics constraints. Its Physics-Residual-Calibrated Upper Confidence Bound (PRC-UCB) acquisition rule combines predicted utility, ensemble disagreement, and a target-temperature physics residual, with nonnegative exploration weights fitted to out-of-fold signed errors. We evaluate the framework on three measured tasks and one simulated task covering binary-mixture viscosity, drug solubility, ionic-liquid viscosity, and electrolyte conductivity. KolTa ranks first or second in mean area under the learning curve (AULC) on every task and outperforms seven of the eight comparator strategies in paired tests, winning 75 of 78 paired comparisons across tasks and seeds against those seven strategies. Across the three measured tasks, its largest gap to the best mean AULC is 0.032, compared with at least 0.056 for every comparator. On Drug, reaching 80% average recovery of the remaining targets across drugs requires an estimated median of 348 additional formulation queries, about 18% fewer than the fastest comparator. Researchers can adapt the framework to diverse formulation problems through component roles and physical constraints.

title: GIST: Gibbs-Targeted Hierarchical Data Selection for Offline RLVR
text: Title: GIST: Gibbs-Targeted Hierarchical Data Selection for Offline RLVR Xuliang Huang , Tianxiang Zhao , Chengwei Qin , Yao Shu Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG) Offline reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains on a fixed pool of sampled responses and typically supervises every token of every response, although responses and tokens are not equally informative. We study which ones to supervise through the Gibbs-optimal policy of KL-regularized RLVR, which offline training targets, and measure the mismatch between a policy and this target with a bidirectional KL divergence. At the reference policy, this mismatch factorizes exactly and separates the two outcomes: correct responses contribute mainly through the forward term, concentrated on their low-probability tokens, and incorrect responses through the reverse term, concentrated on the responses the policy generates often and on their high-probability tokens. Based on this analysis, we propose GIST (Gibbs-Targeted Hierarchical Data Selection), a two-level selection method that approximates these principles with signals available before training. GIST uses the sampling temperature to select correct responses on-policy and incorrect responses near the policy's mode, and it uses the initial policy's token probabilities to supervise only the tokens where the mismatch lies. Applied to two offline training objectives, GIST raises the average accuracy over GSM8K, MATH-500, and MBPP for all three models under both objectives. In a controlled comparison on Qwen3-0.6B/GSM8K, it outperforms seven selection baselines that choose from the same candidates while supervising 66.6% fewer tokens than training on all candidates of the same prompts.

title: Where Should a KV-Cache Repair Budget Go? Distractor Structure and Contextual Compatibility in Non-Prefix Reuse
text: Title: Where Should a KV-Cache Repair Budget Go? Distractor Structure and Contextual Compatibility in Non-Prefix Reuse Yuxing Peng , Zhiqing Tang , Weijia Jia Comments: 36 pages, 6 figures, 34 tables Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) Non-prefix KV-cache reuse encodes retrieved chunks independently and concatenates their caches. To find where a small repair budget should be spent, we vary the chunks around the answer-bearing one (the target) across three 7B-8B models and four datasets of dialogue memory, open-domain QA and API documentation. Reuse loses 19-100% of the context-dependent questions that full prefill answers, and it loses more when the other chunks are of the same kind as the target. Because the recoverable damage is spread over these other chunks, restoring a few of them recovers little, and the budget is better spent on the target. This works through contextual compatibility: recomputing the target against the reused cache beats inserting its full-prefill KV in all seven settings tested, although the recomputed KV stays far from the full-prefill KV. Question attention over reused caches, however, selects the target in at most 18.8% of development questions. A retriever finds it more often, and recomputing its top chunk after moving it next to the question significantly beats InfoFlow-style reordering at the same 5% budget in six of nine open-domain QA and API-documentation settings. On dialogue memory, though, recomputing chunks never significantly beats the token-level selector chosen for each setting.

title: Interpretable Text Embeddings Based on Hierarchical Questions
text: Title: Interpretable Text Embeddings Based on Hierarchical Questions Kohei Oda , Po-Min Chuang , Kiyoaki Shirai , Natthawut Kertkeidkachorn Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) QA-based text embeddings represent texts as vectors consisting of 1/0 answers to yes/no questions. Although these embeddings provide detailed information for interpretation and achieve high task performance, they often require humans to examine a large number of questions. Furthermore, the relationship between the number of questions and the appropriate level of question granularity has not been sufficiently studied. To address these challenges, we propose a method for constructing hierarchical questions for text embeddings. As the hierarchy deepens, questions become more specific and their number increases. During interpretation, we reduce the number of questions that humans need to examine by replacing questions at deeper levels with aligned questions at shallower levels. The question hierarchy is constructed through recursive clustering, contrastive prompting, and question alignment. Experimental results on general-purpose tasks show that our method improves interpretability while maintaining task performance. It is also found that, when only a limited number of questions are available, questions at shallower levels tend to achieve higher task performance than those at deeper levels, even with the same number of questions.

title: Ruby-OPD: Enhancing Pronunciation Controllability and Accuracy for Flow-Matching Text-to-Speech via On-Policy Distillation
text: Title: Ruby-OPD: Enhancing Pronunciation Controllability and Accuracy for Flow-Matching Text-to-Speech via On-Policy Distillation Rui Hu , Xiaolong Lin , Zhenpeng Zhan Comments: 5 pages, 3 tables, work in progress Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) Achieving both high pronunciation accuracy and fine-grained controllability remains a central challenge in Japanese text-to-speech (TTS), as Japanese is an unsegmented language mixing logographic Kanji and phonographic Kana with extensive polyphony. Traditional cascaded systems convert text into phoneme sequences via a front-end, ensuring pronunciation control but discarding lexical semantics and prosodic cues in surface orthography. Conversely, recent zero-shot TTS models directly consume raw orthographic text to improve naturalness, yet suffer from polyphone errors and lack explicit pronunciation control. To bridge this gap, we propose a two-stage framework for flow-matching TTS. First, we investigate Ruby text representations with orthography perturbation to jointly preserve surface forms and target pronunciations for reliable control. Second, we introduce On-Policy Distillation (OPD) on large-scale text-only corpora to enhance pronunciation accuracy on raw orthographic text without paired speech. On the Joyo-Kanji-Yomi benchmark, our model achieves 97.13% Accuracy, 2.02% Target PER, 0.70% Sentence PER, and 4.21% Sentence CER under raw text while retaining strong controllability.

title: A volume-conserving ALE continuous Galerkin method with residual-based Dirichlet--Neumann fluxes for nonlinear free-surface waves
text: Title: A volume-conserving ALE continuous Galerkin method with residual-based Dirichlet--Neumann fluxes for nonlinear free-surface waves Fan Wang , Yinhua Xia , Yan Xu Subjects: Numerical Analysis (math.NA) We develop an arbitrary Lagrangian--Eulerian continuous Galerkin finite element method for two-dimensional fully nonlinear free-surface potential flow. An isoparametric finite element method computes the interior potential on the current fluid domain, while a residual-based Dirichlet--Neumann flux drives the surface evolution. The residual-based flux satisfies a global discrete balance inherited from the interior variational formulation. When combined with compatible mesh motion, surface projection, and quadrature, this balance yields conservation of the discrete fluid volume at the semi-discrete level. An optional volume-conserving sixth-order surface dissipation controls high-frequency oscillations, and the surface equations are advanced with fourth-order Runge--Kutta integration, updating the mesh and interior solution at every stage. Numerical experiments confirm the expected spatial convergence for linear free-surface waves and demonstrate reduced mesh sensitivity for nonlinear waves over flat and curved bottoms. A rotating-wavemaker example further illustrates the treatment of moving solid boundaries.

title: Zero-Shot Coordination among LLM Agents
text: Title: Zero-Shot Coordination among LLM Agents Adrian Hayler , Shashank Reddy Chirra , Andrei Lupu , Johannes Forkel , Bidipta Sarkar , Siheng Feng , Jakob Foerster Comments: NeurIPS 2026 Poster. ICLR 26 MALGAI Workshop Oral. The first two authors contributed equally Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) We study zero-shot coordination (ZSC), where independently developed agents must coordinate at test time. While ZSC has been well studied in the RL literature, far less is known about the performance of LLM agents despite their increasing deployment in such settings. Existing work on LLM coordination often relies on specialised scaffolding that independently developed agents are unlikely to share in practice. Moreover, evaluations on complex environments (e.g., Hanabi) make it difficult to pinpoint the sources of coordination failure. In contrast, we focus on simple, general-purpose scaffolds in minimal environments designed to isolate specific coordination challenges. Our results show that even in these controlled settings, frontier LLM agents struggle to coordinate, largely due to limited understanding of the coordination problem and weak reasoning about their partner's beliefs. While LLMs introduce semantic information as an additional axis for coordination, they nonetheless fail to exploit this structure effectively. Towards this, we propose Coordination-friendly definitions (CFDs) as a principled approach for enabling robust coordination among LLM agents. Finally, we show that CFDs can be discovered automatically, removing the need for manual engineering. Code is available at this https URL .

title: Polynomial $(2α+\varepsilon)$- and Quadratic $4$-Approximation Algorithms for the Biased Traveling Salesman Problem in Bipartitioned Networks
text: Title: Polynomial $(2α+\varepsilon)$- and Quadratic $4$-Approximation Algorithms for the Biased Traveling Salesman Problem in Bipartitioned Networks Jingyang Zhao , Trung Q. Duong , Een-Kee Hong , Hyundong Shin Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS) The traveling salesman problem (TSP) is one of the fundamental problems in combinatorial optimization that asks for a minimum-cost Hamiltonian cycle in a complete undirected graph with $N$ vertices. For the metric TSP, where edge costs satisfy the triangle inequality, a long line of work has produced constant-factor approximation algorithms, culminating in the best-known approximation ratio $\alpha<3/2-10^{-36}$. The biased TSP (BTSP) generalizes the metric TSP to bipartitioned networks: the vertex set is partitioned into two subsets, edge costs satisfy the triangle inequality within each subset, while edges crossing the partition may violate it by a certain bias factor. This model captures heterogeneous routing scenarios in which distances are metric only locally but may be distorted across different regions or vertex types. Previously, the only known result for the BTSP was a $7/2$-approximation algorithm with running time $O(N^3)$. In this paper, we present two new approximation algorithms that significantly improve the state of the art. The first achieves an approximation ratio of $2\alpha+\varepsilon$ (strictly less than $3$) in polynomial time $N^{O(1)}$ for any constant $\varepsilon>0$, where the exponent grows at least linearly with $1/\varepsilon$. The second achieves a $4$-approximation in only $O(N^2)$ running time, reducing the previous cubic-time bound by a full polynomial factor. These advances directly support emerging networked systems---including multi-tier 6G architectures and hybrid quantum-classical networks---where cross-region transitions incur biased and non-metric overheads.

title: A Bag of Tricks for Defending Deep Learning-based Face Recognition Pipelines against Backdoor Attacks
text: Title: A Bag of Tricks for Defending Deep Learning-based Face Recognition Pipelines against Backdoor Attacks Quentin Le Roux , Marti Jimenez , Yannick Teglia , Philippe Loubet Moundi Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Machine Learning (cs.LG) The protection of mature, multi-stage Face Recognition Systems is crucial to system providers. This technical report targets the threat model most relevant to industry practitioners: although model training is performed in-house, training data is sourced from possibly-compromised third parties. Given this setting, we present three practical defense "tricks" against data poisoning-based backdoor attacks. The first operates at training-time, detecting poisoned identities during training or prior to a pipeline's deployment. The last two operate at inference-time, filtering suspicious inputs before an answer can be sent back to a potential attacker. Each method is presented with their motivation, algorithms and computational impact, and evaluated on realistic face recognition workloads. Our goal is to provide actionable hardening techniques to system providers.

title: Twists and Turns: A Graph-Based Benchmark and Framework for Long-Term Memory in Exploration Tasks
text: Title: Twists and Turns: A Graph-Based Benchmark and Framework for Long-Term Memory in Exploration Tasks Chongyuan Dai , Yaling Shen , Zirui Song , Junfeng Liao , Jinpeng Hu , Xiuying Chen Comments: 29 pages, 5 figures Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) Long-term problem-solving processes, such as scientific research and software development, proceed along an evolving trial-and-error trajectory toward a central goal. We term these \textit{exploration tasks}, which require models to remember not only facts but also how solutions are tested against intermediate outcomes and early attempts are continually revised or revived. However, existing long-term memory research focuses on factual recall and updates, overlooking the interconnected nature of exploration. We observe that exploration processes naturally form graphs, with branching approaches linked by revisions and reconsiderations. Motivated by this, we propose \textsc{LExMem}, a graph-guided benchmark designed to evaluate \underline{\textsc{Mem}}ory in \underline{\textsc{L}}ong-term \underline{\textsc{Ex}}ploration tasks. We model exploration processes as graphs and introduce an evolutionary mechanism to increase their structural complexity, yielding 224 dialogues and 2,018 question-answer instances derived from graph structures. Building on the same insight, we propose \textsc{LExGraph}, a graph-based memory framework that incrementally organizes dialogues into interconnected memory nodes and retrieves evidence through hybrid retrieval and neighbor expansion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that \textsc{LExMem} poses a significant challenge to existing retrieval- and memory-based systems, whereas \textsc{LExGraph} achieves superior performance and generalizes effectively to external benchmarks. Codes and datasets are available at this https URL .

title: Entropogram-guided Visual Realignment Decoding: Capturing the Rhythm of Multimodal Reasoning
text: Title: Entropogram-guided Visual Realignment Decoding: Capturing the Rhythm of Multimodal Reasoning Jiaqi Deng , Zhe Fu , Yakun Chen , Dichang Zhang , Zonghan Wu , Xiaoshui Huang , Huan Huo , Guandong Xu Comments: 22 pages, 9 figures Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Multimedia (cs.MM) Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable progress on cross-modal reasoning tasks, yet they continue to suffer from hallucinations in long-chain reasoning processes. In this work, we revisit hallucination in MLLMs from the perspective of reasoning generation dynamics. We argue that entropy is not merely a static measure of uncertainty but a structured signal that reflects how modality information is integrated throughout decoding. Through systematic analysis, we identify two characteristic entropy patterns associated with hallucination behaviors: (1) a generally high-confidence regime corresponds to premature convergence to inappropriate multimodal interactions; and (2) local abrupt entropy transitions are associated with reasoning instability and hallucination onset. Building on these observations, we propose an entropy-aware self-introspective framework for MLLM reasoning. Our method continuously tracks entropy dynamics during decoding and performs targeted visual re-alignment when suspicious hallucination states are detected, encouraging the model to re-examine salient visual evidence at critical reasoning stages. Extensive experiments across six multimodal reasoning benchmarks spanning nine distinct evaluation settings demonstrate that our approach delivers robust improvements in reasoning accuracy and hallucination robustness, while providing new insights into the generation dynamics underlying MLLM failures. The code is available at: this https URL .

title: Unaligned Image Guided Denoising via Cross-modal Conditional Flow Matching
text: Title: Unaligned Image Guided Denoising via Cross-modal Conditional Flow Matching Runmin Zhang , Linshan Li , Si-Yuan Cao , Zhu Yu , Lingyu Zhu , Huaqi Zhang , Hui-Liang Shen Comments: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026 Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) This work presents UGD-FM, a novel unaligned image guided denoising framework based on cross-modal conditional flow matching. Unlike previous approaches that assume spatially aligned inputs or only handle small-baseline rectified pairs, we address a more challenging setting where severe target noise and large-range two-dimensional cross-modal misalignment coexist. Specifically, we formulate guided denoising as a progressive flow matching process, allowing image restoration and aligned guidance aggregation to mutually reinforce each other. To support efficient few-step inference, we introduce a stage-focused and inference-consistent training strategy that focuses on task-critical denoising stages, and mitigates the training-inference mismatch. We further propose adaptive sparse guidance propagation for efficient and reliable large-range matching, regularized by perceptual and geometric auxiliary losses. Experiments demonstrate that UGD-FM achieves state-of-the-art denoising performance with only one or two inference steps, and is compatible with modern single-image restoration backbones.

title: D3D: Decoupled Diffusion Drafting for Asynchronous Speculative Decoding
text: Title: D3D: Decoupled Diffusion Drafting for Asynchronous Speculative Decoding Baoyou Chen , Ruiqiao Mei , Guancong Lin , Tao Song , Weihao Yuan , Qun Liu , Siyu Zhu Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG) Target-conditioned diffusion drafters predict candidate tokens in parallel, yet each new block must wait for updated target-model hidden states. This forces drafting and verification to run sequentially, limiting speedup even though each block is generated in one pass. We introduce D3D, a standalone diffusion drafter that removes this inter-round dependency. D3D combines blockwise denoising with auxiliary autoregressive supervision to achieve long accepted prefixes without target hidden states. This independence lets D3D draft successor blocks during verification in one packed pass, enabling asynchronous speculative decoding. We progressively prune layers according to their effect on acceptance length to reduce the cost of packed drafting. Removing five of 36 layers retains over 99\% of mean acceptance length across three benchmarks with Qwen3-8B as the target. Across seven benchmarks, D3D averages 5.00$\times$ and 5.71$\times$ decoding speedup with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B targets, compared with 4.03$\times$ and 3.67$\times$ for DFlash. On GSM8K with Qwen3-32B, speedup reaches 7.48$\times$. Code is publicly available at this https URL .

title: Partially Interpretable Decision Trees
text: Title: Partially Interpretable Decision Trees Ludovic Schwartz , Federico Berton , Tim van Erven Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) Partially interpretable models extend simple interpretable models with the option to defer complicated inputs to an accurate but uninterpretable black-box model. By deferring more inputs, the model gets more accurate; by deferring fewer, it gets more interpretable. Existing procedures to train such partially interpretable models build on linear models or decision rules. We propose three algorithms for decision trees: a partially interpretable extension of the existing Branches algorithm, which performs exact search to optimize the tree; a conversion algorithm that we run on top of standard CART, which is computationally more efficient; and a generalized CART whose splitting criterion takes into account the option to defer while growing the tree. Perhaps surprisingly, the performance of the three algorithms is similar across many realworld datasets. We can explain this through a formal bound on the potential gain of smart tree construction, provided the black box accuracy is sufficiently homogeneous across the domain. We also construct a synthetic dataset where the accuracy of the black box is deliberately inhomogeneous. There, our deferral-aware generalization of CART does outperform regular CART and matches the performance of exact search. Finally, we evaluate an application to concept bottleneck models. Partially interpretable decision trees can replace uninterpretable neural networks after the bottleneck. On undeferred inputs, the model is fully interpretable, and deferring preserves accuracy.

title: Neural Network-based Control Systems with Application to Flight Control, From Classical Neural Control to Reinforcement Learning
text: Title: Neural Network-based Control Systems with Application to Flight Control, From Classical Neural Control to Reinforcement Learning Seyyed Ali Emami , Paolo Castaldi , Mohammad Narimani , Mahdi Shahrajabian , Mostafa Ezabadi , Alireza Ettelaei , Hosein Saadatmanesh , Zahra Shahbazi Subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY) This book provides a comprehensive and systematic exploration of neural network-based intelligent control systems for aerospace applications, bridging foundational theory with practical implementation. It is structured into two primary parts: Part I covers model-based control design, detailing Feedback Error Learning (FEL), pseudocontrol strategies, and neural backstepping for strict-feedback systems, along with practical refinements such as learning rule modifications, composite learning, and discrete-time formulations, all grounded in rigorous Lyapunov stability analysis. Part II introduces model-free control, laying the groundwork for Reinforcement Learning and Approximate Dynamic Programming. Throughout, theoretical concepts are solidified through detailed case studies on quadrotor UAVs, fixed-wing aircraft (GTM), satellites, and hypersonic flight vehicles, complete with performance metrics, parameter sensitivity analyses, and discussions of actuator faults, input constraints, and wind disturbances, making the book an invaluable resource for students and practicing engineers seeking to design, simulate, and analyze intelligent flight control systems.

title: DreamRealm: Exploring and Materializing Hallucination Worlds for Trustworthy Vision-Language Models
text: Title: DreamRealm: Exploring and Materializing Hallucination Worlds for Trustworthy Vision-Language Models Benlei Cui , Chunyang Chai , Yiliang Zhang , Xiaoqian Xia , Chengwen Yao , Song Li , Longtao Huang , Yuwen Zhai , Haiwen Hong Comments: 28 pages, including supplementary material. Code: this https URL . Model: this https URL Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remain prone to visual hallucinations when correct responses depend on subtle visual details. One line of post-training methods constructs visual contrasts through image retrieval, generation, or editing to improve fine-grained perception. However, these contrasts are not built around the model's own hallucinations, making it difficult to ensure that supervision targets its actual perceptual confusions. Another line suppresses hallucinated outputs through response correction or preference learning under fixed image conditions, but leaves the design of supervision signals on the image-input side underexplored. Inspired by how humans correct misconceptions, we introduce DreamRealm, a post-training framework that explores diverse latent hallucinated responses, minimally edits original images to make them valid, and trains the model to assign each response to its supporting image. Our data construction pipeline, RealmForgePipe, mines observed and latent hallucinations from a target model and materializes them through image editing. Using hallucinations mined from Qwen3.5-9B, we construct the Realized Hallucination Dataset (RealmSet). Our training objective, RealmMatch, constructs a likelihood score matrix across image--response combinations and combines supervised learning with bidirectional contrastive losses to reinforce correct matches and suppress mismatches. Compared with the original Qwen3.5-9B model, DreamRealm improves performance across six visual perception and hallucination benchmarks, including gains of 7.26 percentage points in HallusionBench accuracy and 11.34 percentage points in MMVP pair accuracy. Together with ablation studies on data construction and training methods, these results demonstrate that hallucination assignment is a promising paradigm for improving visual perception and mitigating hallucinations.

title: EviSeek: An Evidence-Centric Agentic Framework for Embodied Active Information Seeking
text: Title: EviSeek: An Evidence-Centric Agentic Framework for Embodied Active Information Seeking Jintao Li , Zhiyong Cao , Baihua Xiao , Yu Bai , Börje F. Karlsson Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) Active embodied question answering requires agents to acquire evidence through viewpoint changes and physical interaction. The central challenge is to avoid undirected interaction: taking plausible actions without specifying what evidence they should reveal for answering the question. Action plans and accumulated histories alone can leave the informational purpose of an interaction implicit. We introduce EviSeek, a training-free framework that makes question-derived evidence demands explicit acquisition objectives, linking observation-conditioned actions and selectively retained evidence to the information the agent seeks. On 3,436 ESI-Bench questions, EviSeek improves accuracy over the Single-model agent by 7.1 percentage points with Qwen3-VL-32B and 3.7 points with Gemini 3.1 Pro, while improving visual-support-weighted accuracy and reducing mean token usage. These findings support making the informational purpose of interaction explicit, with action selection and evidence retention organized around what the agent needs to learn to answer the question.

title: Hardwired Distributed Processing Units for Inference: Neural Decisions at the Sensor that Free the Host
text: Title: Hardwired Distributed Processing Units for Inference: Neural Decisions at the Sensor that Free the Host Raj Mali Comments: 8 pages, 9 figures, 11 tables. Companion to arXiv:2610.33107 and arXiv:2610.38752 Subjects: Hardware Architecture (cs.AR) ; Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Machine Learning (cs.LG) We show that a hardwired distributed processing unit (HDPU) can take a neural decision at the sensor and so remove the inference from the host. Built for zebra-crossing detection on a low-cost Artix-7 FPGA, the unit decides on every camera frame in a fixed 2,269,477 clock cycles (34.04 ms depends upon Fpga clk ), inside the 37.49-ms frame period, and on the board it returns the same scores and decisions as its bit-exact software model on all 639 test images. The whole detection path, from camera pixels to decision, takes 1,814 LUTs, with no processor, no operating system and no full-resolution frame store. When the unit answers instead of reporting "not sure", 95.7% of its answers on street photographs are correct, and a hardware contrast stage lifts accuracy on camera-like dashcam frames from 47.7% to 78.2%. The host is spared all of the inference: 8.13 ms of a core in every frame period, where a full-precision ResNet-18 would need more than a frame period even on 16 threads. It also receives 16 bytes per frame instead of 614,400, 38,400 times less. The unit is an 80x60-pixel pipeline feeding a four-layer binarized CNN with 93,408 one-bit weights, verified bit-exactly from a Python model through RTL simulation to the board. Earlier HDPUs did pre-processing (edges, corners, steering); this one shows that the decision itself can move to the sensor.

title: Understanding the Out-of-Distribution Generalization of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in LLMs
text: Title: Understanding the Out-of-Distribution Generalization of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in LLMs Nuo-Jing Liang , Xiao-Tong Yuan , Pan Zhou Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Machine Learning (stat.ML) Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning substantially improves Large Language Models (LLMs), yet its out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization mechanism remains theoretically underexplored. We study CoT as compositional OOD generalization: the target task lacks complete reasoning trajectories or direct input-output pairs, while training provides only in-distribution (ID) atomic step data. We show that CoT generalizes by repeatedly applying a shared single-step predictor to compose reusable ID transitions. Theoretically, let $T$ denote the number of reasoning steps in the target task, $n$ the number of training samples per sub-task, and $k$ the number of output tokens per step; then the OOD task risk is controlled by the sum of the ID sub-task risks, scaled by a coefficient of order $\mathcal{O}(k)$ that is independent of $T$, although the summed risk itself may still grow with $T$. A Rademacher-complexity analysis further shows that the estimation term is of order $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T/n})$, rather than linear in $T$, due to predictor sharing under a uniform capacity control on the shared class. For autoregressive Next-Token Prediction, the final-task risk is bounded by the best-in-class step-level risk scaled by the same coefficient of order $\mathcal{O}(k)$, plus an estimation term of order $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(k\sqrt{T/n}\big)$. A parity-coupled construction further shows that, for the sub-task empirical risk minimizer, the expected final-task risk is at least the best in-class risk plus $\Omega(\sqrt{T/n})$ when $T\le n$. Experiments on Atom-Task and GSM8K support the theory: CoT enables short-to-long and compositional generalization, while explicit state tracking is crucial. Our code is available at this https URL .

title: Graph Foundation Models Can Become Effective Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detectors
text: Title: Graph Foundation Models Can Become Effective Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detectors Zhuangyan Hu , Zhuoxuan Liang , Wei Li , Xiaohua Jia , Moustafa Youssef , Sumi Helal Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) Multivariate time series anomaly detection (MTSAD) relies on modeling both temporal dynamics and inter-sensor dependencies to identify complex system faults. Although graph-based detectors explicitly model sensor topologies, they train task-specific networks from scratch on limited target-domain data, remaining vulnerable to spurious correlations and unable to reuse transferable priors. While pretrained Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) offer transferable topological priors and anomaly discriminability, directly adapting them to MTSAD is hindered by cross-modal feature-topology mismatch, unreliable pseudo-anomaly supervision, and decision distortion during node-to-window aggregation. To fill these gaps, we propose a novel adaptation framework, Gfm4Mtsad, which unleashes pretrained GFMs for MTSAD. We introduce the Structure-and-Information Contract Alignment (SICA) module to bridge continuous time series and the pretrained GFM space. This module harmonizes principal subspace token projection, normal-prior-guided graph construction, and residual recovery to suppress spurious edges while retaining fine-grained temporal details. We propose a Mechanism-Aligned Pseudo-Anomaly Screening strategy (MAPS) to steer unsupervised learning. It applies localized dependency breaks while preserving empirical residuals, selecting hard negatives near the normal boundary for targeted supervision. We develop a Tail-Gated Evidence Calibration mechanism (TGEC) to eliminate node-to-window aggregation distortion. It calibrates multi-granular graph responses against normal operational references, strictly preserving benign score rankings while selectively refining extreme anomaly candidates in the tail distribution for reliable window detection and interpretable sensor evidence. Extensive evaluations with two GFM backbones demonstrate that Gfm4Mtsad achieves superior detection performance over existing baselines.

title: TwinBridge: Digital Twin-Driven Policy and Reward Transfer for Real-World Reinforcement Learning in Laboratory Robotics
text: Title: TwinBridge: Digital Twin-Driven Policy and Reward Transfer for Real-World Reinforcement Learning in Laboratory Robotics Shu'ang Sun , Yibo Qiu , Haoliang Ye , Zan Huang , Ao Tian , Kan Ding , Ronald Xu , Mingzhai Sun Comments: 8 pages, 6 figures Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) Online reinforcement learning offers an effective approach to precise laboratory manipulation, yet costly real-world demonstrations and limited access to dense process rewards hinder its practical application. We present TwinBridge, a digital twin-driven framework that supplies policy initialization and dense visual rewards for real-world online learning. We construct digital twins by combining 3D Gaussian splatting with physics simulation. Here, simulator states provide task events and geometric progress under physical prerequisites and ordering constraints, yielding rewards for policy pretraining with simulated demonstrations and reinforcement learning. We distill this supervision into a visual reward model. During real-world interaction, its predictions are combined with execution history to compute dense rewards for human-in-the-loop policy refinement. Across five real-world laboratory tasks, TwinBridge achieves a final mean autonomous success rate of 98% with at most 25 minutes of real-world interaction per task. Experiments show that dense rewards improve interaction efficiency over sparse rewards, and simulation-based policy initialization further accelerates learning.

title: EvoGuard: Mitigating Degradation in Online Skill Evolution
text: Title: EvoGuard: Mitigating Degradation in Online Skill Evolution Yanli Wang , Zichen Bai , Tianyue Jiang , Kunming Shao , Junhao Shi , Xueqin Liu , Jinguo Sun , Muye Li , Tingting Bi , Yanlin Wang , Shaoqiang Zheng , Xuefei Diao , Zhuwei Zeng , Nan Duan , Peng Cao Comments: 16 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables, including appendices Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) Skills let language agents reuse experience across tasks as natural-language documents. Recent work evolves skills from interaction, but existing methods have limitations when skills evolve online. Prior methods update a skill offline from a batch of trajectories collected over many tasks. Some then adopt the new skill without any check, which can degrade the skill over time. Others keep it only if it improves performance on a held-out validation set, which is too slow and costly to run after every update. We introduce EvoGuard, a pairwise skill selector that mitigates skill degradation at low latency and cost. We first run the agent iteratively to build pools of skills and score each skill on a private test set to obtain utility labels. We pair the skills and use rejection sampling to keep only pairs with a clear utility gap. The selector is trained on the logits of two label tokens to pick the better skill. At deployment it decides in a single forward pass, which is significantly faster than evaluation on the private test set. Compared with adopting every new skill, EvoGuard improves success by 11.0% on ALFWorld, 5.9% on ScienceWorld, and 2.7% on LiveCodeBench.

title: SUMONE: A Simple and Efficient Summarizer for Plug-and-Play Agent Memory
text: Title: SUMONE: A Simple and Efficient Summarizer for Plug-and-Play Agent Memory Jizhe Zhang , Ang Li , Chenheng Zhang , Yisen Wang Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) Long-horizon language-model agents accumulate increasingly large interaction histories, making context compaction essential for efficient execution. Existing learned compaction methods often rely on downstream task outcomes or solver behavior, coupling training to specific tasks or agents. We introduce SumOne, a standalone summarizer trained to preserve information in agent histories through masked reconstruction. Given a summary of the expired history, a frozen reconstructor recovers randomly masked portions of the original trajectory; reconstruction quality, combined with a length penalty, provides a task-agnostic reward for optimizing the summarizer with GRPO. This yields self-supervision directly from raw trajectories, without reference summaries or downstream task execution. At inference time, only the lightweight summarizer is retained, enabling plug-and-play context compression for otherwise unchanged agents. We conduct a systematic evaluation of SumOne in long-horizon search and software-engineering tasks. SumOne reduces estimated inference cost by approximately 78\% on DeepSearchQA and 75\% on SWE-bench Verified relative to operating with full context, with absolute decreases of 0.04. The same checkpoint also transfers across downstream models and agent harnesses without additional fine-tuning.

title: $A^3$-VLA: Automatic Perception-Guided Attention Alignment for Robot Manipulation
text: Title: $A^3$-VLA: Automatic Perception-Guided Attention Alignment for Robot Manipulation Shengzhe Zhang , Qi Zhang , Dazhong Shen , Chao Wang , Shaopeng Zhai , Hui Xiong Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) enable robots to perform manipulation tasks by leveraging Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to process visual observations and language instructions. However, the action prediction objective itself lacks fine-grained task-specific perceptual supervision, making it prone to relying on task-irrelevant visual shortcuts, leading attention away from target objects and key interaction areas, thereby limiting its operational performance and generalization ability. To address this, we propose Automatic Perception-Guided Attention Alignment for Robot Manipulation ($A^3$-VLA), a framework that derives task-specific visual guidance from the manipulation process itself. Specifically, $A^3$-VLA first generates heuristic candidate regions for target objects and the robot from interaction-induced visual changes, and refines them with a visual segmentation model offline. These regions serve as explicit perceptual guidance through two complementary objectives: an attention allocation loss that encourages sufficient focus on task-critical regions when language or robot state tokens query the visual input, and a contrastive learning loss that aligns the representations of candidate target regions with language instructions while separating them from task-irrelevant regions. Extensive experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that $A^3$-VLA consistently improves multiple VLA backbones, with an average success rate gain of 6.5% - 25.2% across benchmarks.

title: AmbiHTMLBench: A Benchmark for HTML-based Visually Rich Document parsing
text: Title: AmbiHTMLBench: A Benchmark for HTML-based Visually Rich Document parsing Boyu Niu , Yingjie Xiong , Shurui Li , Linhan Pang , Yuntong Zhang , Han Wang , Hao Wu , Kai Zuo , Xu Tang , Xuanhe Zhou , Fan Wu Comments: Check latest benchmark info on this https URL Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) Traditional document parsing systems use Markdown as their output representation, which is effective for linear text but does not fully preserve fine-grained spatial structure, table geometry, visual hierarchy, or rendering semantics. We show that HTML is advantageous for heterogeneous and layout-sensitive documents whose representations must remain editable, inspectable, and reusable, and introduce AmbiHTMLBench to systematically study this setting. In this benchmark, given a real-world document, a model must recover executable HTML that preserves its content, organization, and visual appearance. The benchmark contains 1,115 diverse pages with structured annotations and evaluates predictions in two different ways: The objective protocol aligns ground-truth and predicted rendered blocks and measures table fidelity, page-level text error, and a two-dimensional layout consistency; a complementary reference-anchored protocol measures perceived fidelity by aligning LLM judges with human preferences. Across ten primary multimodal systems, the best objective score is 0.8092, while the subjective winner is different, demonstrating that automatic decomposition and human-perceived fidelity capture complementary properties. We further fine-tune a small-parameter expert model and find that task-specific adaptation yields good performance on document-to-HTML reconstruction task. These results position AmbiHTMLBench as a diagnostic testbed for building smarter and more logical document parsing systems.

title: Timed Games under Environmental Interference with Real-Time Objectives
text: Title: Timed Games under Environmental Interference with Real-Time Objectives Andrea Manini , Matteo Rossi , Pierluigi San Pietro Subjects: Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO) Classical Timed Games formulations may be unsuitable, or require substantial modeling effort, to capture complex interaction patterns between a controller and its surrounding environment, in which non-determinism must be resolved after the controller has chosen which action to perform. In this paper, we develop the theory of Timed CLTLoc Games (TCGs), a Timed Game variant designed to facilitate the modeling of such patterns. Unlike classical Timed Games formulations, TCGs partition locations rather than transitions, and use Constraint Linear Temporal Logic over clocks (CLTLoc) to specify the controller's objectives. We develop algorithms for solving TCGs and synthesizing winning controller strategies for games whose objectives include formal properties such as reachability and safety. For reachability objectives, our synthesis algorithm yields winning controller strategies that minimize the number of moves required to reach a goal state. Solving reachability TCGs is EXPTIME-complete, matching the complexity of solving reachability Timed Games. All of our algorithms operate backwards and are implemented in our C++ region-based library TARZAN, leveraging OpenMP for efficient parallelization. Experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of TARZAN.

title: Fourier Entropy Bounds via Approximations
text: Title: Fourier Entropy Bounds via Approximations Manaswi Paraashar , Nitin Saurabh Subjects: Computational Complexity (cs.CC) We establish upper bounds on the Shannon entropy $\mathbb H(\widehat f^{\,2})$ of the Fourier distribution of Boolean functions. We prove that $$ \mathbb H(\widehat f^{\,2}) =O\!\left(\log\bigl(1+\|\widehat f\|_{1,1/3}\bigr)\right), $$ where $\|\widehat f\|_{1,1/3}$ denotes the minimum spectral norm of a pointwise $1/3$-approximant to $f$. This implies $\mathbb H(\widehat f^{\,2})=O(\mathsf R^\oplus(f))$, where $\mathsf R^\oplus(f)$ is bounded-error randomized parity-query complexity. We also bound Fourier entropy by the smaller of the two one-sided average unambiguous parity-certificate complexities. More generally, for any exact representation of indicator of $f$ as $\sum_C w_C\mathbf1_C$, with nonnegative weights and affine subspaces $C$, we prove $$ \mathbb H(\widehat f^{\,2}) =O\!\left(\sum_C w_C\,2^{-k_C}k_C\right), \qquad k_C=\operatorname{codim}(C). $$ The quantity on the right is the average conical junta degree of the representation. These results strengthen earlier bounds of (Arunachalam et al. 2021) by extending approximation-based entropy estimates to Shannon entropy and allowing one-sided and overlapping exact representations. The proofs use an entropy bound from a sequence of increasingly accurate approximants of $f$ with \emph{small} spectral norm. Our techniques also find an application in quantum communication complexity, where it improves a lower bound for the bounded-error quantum communication complexity of XOR functions.

title: Within-Family EfficientNet Scaling under Fixed-Resolution Transfer Learning for Spectral-Domain Optical Coherence Tomography Retinal Disease Classification
text: Title: Within-Family EfficientNet Scaling under Fixed-Resolution Transfer Learning for Spectral-Domain Optical Coherence Tomography Retinal Disease Classification Shkelqim Sherifi Comments: 46 pages, 20 figures, 18 tables Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG) Background/Objectives: CNNs perform well in retinal disease classification from spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT), but whether EfficientNet's natural-image scaling hierarchy transfers to medical-image transfer learning at fixed resolution remains unclear. This study evaluates EfficientNet-B0-B7 for four-class SD-OCT classification and accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. Methods: Eight ImageNet-pretrained variants (4.05-64.10M instantiated backbone parameters) were evaluated at 224x224 on the Kermany dataset. Grayscale images were replicated to RGB and processed using model-embedded preprocessing and augmentation. Training comprised frozen-backbone head training followed by partial fine-tuning. Metrics covered classification, discrimination, efficiency, and visual analyses. Results: Test accuracy varied non-monotonically from 95.93% (B0) to 96.95% (B1); B7 achieved 96.73%. B1 had the highest accuracy and Drusen F1 (0.8780), while B7 had Drusen F1 of 0.8720 and the highest Drusen recall (0.9177). Drusen had the lowest F1 across all variants and contributed 82.2% of the summed squared deviation in class-specific F1; class ranking remained Normal > CNV > DME > Drusen. The OCT accuracy ranking differed from the reported ImageNet hierarchy, where B7 ranked first. The accuracy-to-parameter ratio fell from 19.82 to 1.48 percentage points per million total parameters. The final train-test gap had a weak, non-significant association with test accuracy (r = 0.26, p = 0.53). Conclusions: Larger EfficientNet variants did not consistently improve SD-OCT classification. B1 achieved the highest accuracy and Drusen F1, whereas B7 showed a secondary accuracy recovery at greater model size and CPU latency, indicating task and protocol dependent scaling effects. As cross-partition duplicates have not been independently audited, results are conditional on the supplied split.

title: Beyond Infraction Scores: Failure-Boundary Profiles for Closed-Loop Evaluation of Driving and Robot Navigation Agents
text: Title: Beyond Infraction Scores: Failure-Boundary Profiles for Closed-Loop Evaluation of Driving and Robot Navigation Agents Milan Bulat , Gino Ardelean , Ellington Kirby Comments: 16 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables. Code: this https URL . Data: this https URL Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Software Engineering (cs.SE) Closed-loop driving benchmarks in CARLA rank agents by a driving score that multiplies route completion by an infraction penalty. This score does not distinguish an agent that stops in front of an obstacle from one that pushes past it. In a corridor closed by two parked cars, for example, one agent that drives through with contact averages 52.2 on the blocked widths, while the agents that stop average between 37.8 and 40.6. We propose failure-boundary profiles, an evaluation in which each scenario family varies one measured factor, such as corridor width or the time gap in oncoming traffic, and each variant is certified from measurement as one where the agent should proceed or one where it should stop. Along this axis we estimate two curves per agent, commitment (the probability of attempting the passage) and competence (the probability of passing without contact), and locate where each crosses one half, with intervals that account for the simulator's run-to-run variance. The certified labels also give a summary metric, decision accuracy, which credits clean passes on passable variants and stops on blocked ones. We evaluate seven driving agents on seven CARLA families. The rule-based expert reaches a decision accuracy of 0.74 and TFv6, the highest-scoring learned agent, 0.60. Agents with similar driving scores fail in different ways, and agents that reliably stop at a blocked corridor still rarely wait for a gap in oncoming traffic. We also apply the method, unchanged, to a warehouse robot in Isaac Sim. The navigation policy we test stops at blocked gaps in only one of three families, and two fine-tuned versions of it pass more gaps cleanly but no longer stop at all.

title: CoDecide: Content-Adaptive Video Decoding for High-Throughput Video Analytics
text: Title: CoDecide: Content-Adaptive Video Decoding for High-Throughput Video Analytics Shristy Shah , Thomas B. Moeslund , Kamal Nasrollahi Comments: Accepted at WACV 2027. 12 pages including supplementary material Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) Analytics on video archives are bottlenecked by decoding. In a dense pipeline that runs a detector on every frame, decoding is a small fraction of the runtime, but once the detector is restricted to selected frames, decoding takes over as the main cost. We introduce CoDecide, a retrospective analytics system that only decodes the frames where new content appears, using signals from the compressed bitstream to find them. Motion tells us something is moving, but not whether it is new to the scene or has been there the whole time. To make that distinction, we supervise a lightweight compressed-domain student on a label-free novelty signal from a frozen DINOv2 teacher, which fires on semantically new regions rather than on any motion. Consequently, the student model generalizes to new camera deployments without requiring per-camera retraining. At inference, it decides which frames to decode and which regions to reconstruct. Detections from the decoded frames are propagated to the skipped frames using motion vectors. We evaluate CoDecide with a leave-one-dataset-out protocol on VIRAT, MEVA, and ShanghaiTech. Against a dense per-frame detector, CoDecide recovers more moving-object detections than prior compressed-domain selectors at an equivalent decoding budget, outperforming even a competitor trained directly on the target camera. CoDecide runs 15 to 24x faster than a pipeline that decodes and detects every frame. Code is available at this https URL .

title: Generative Learning on Dynamic Text-Attributed Graphs
text: Title: Generative Learning on Dynamic Text-Attributed Graphs Zhenyu Yang , Yuhong Chen , Binli Luo , Xiaodong Li , Xiaolin Hu , Hui Li , Jintang Li Comments: 10 pages, 7 figures, 7 tables Subjects: Social and Information Networks (cs.SI) Dynamic text-attributed graphs capture evolving interactions among entities with rich textual information, but future-link prediction remains difficult when nodes have little interaction history or appear as new targets. We propose \method, a generative framework that represents nodes with compact semantic identifiers (SIDs) learned from text and autoregressively predicts a target SID conditioned on the source SID, recent interaction events, and relative time gaps. A lightweight structural calibration further incorporates repetition, co-occurrence, and popularity. At inference time, \method encodes each query context once and reuses SID likelihoods to rank prescribed candidates, providing a candidate-efficient prediction interface. Experiments on nine datasets show broadly competitive performance across domains and graph densities. Source-side inductive evaluations demonstrate that text-derived SIDs provide a useful representation when a test source has no observed interaction history, while two recommendation-oriented case studies evaluate controlled new-user adaptation and first-arrival ranking for inductive new items. Further analyses characterize SID uniqueness, capacity, and temporal stability. Overall, the results support combining text-derived SIDs with temporal histories for dynamic link prediction.

title: eBPF-Driven Adaptive Lifetime-Aware Data Placement for Shared FDP SSDs
text: Title: eBPF-Driven Adaptive Lifetime-Aware Data Placement for Shared FDP SSDs Hajin Moon , Taewan Noh , Chaeeun Yoon , Jeonghun Lee , Junyoung Han , Joo-Young Hwang , Youngjae Kim Subjects: Operating Systems (cs.OS) NVMe Flexible Data Placement (FDP) reduces SSD write amplification by separating data with different lifetimes to minimize garbage collection (GC) copying. However, on shared servers, multiple tenants generate more lifetime classes than the available placement handles. Existing approaches rely on static mappings or application-specific knowledge, failing to capture runtime lifetimes and adapt to changing workloads. The challenge is to identify which data die together and determine which classes should be separated to maximize GC savings under a limited handle budget. We present eFDP, an eBPF-based system that automatically learns data lifetimes and manages FDP placement for unmodified applications on a stock Linux kernel. By tracking writes and invalidations, eFDP identifies lifetime classes and estimates the GC copying saved by separating them. It first assigns each tenant a handle, then allocates the remaining handles to the separations offering the greatest savings. It also re-plans placement when active tenants change. With four database tenants on an emulated FDP SSD, eFDP eliminates twice as much excess write amplification as tenant-level isolation and improves every writing tenant's throughput by 19-23%. On an enterprise FDP SSD, given RocksDB's levels, it matches a manually optimized placement using three handles instead of five. After a tenant switch, eFDP re-plans within seven minutes and maintains 25% lower write amplification than the original layout even after an hour.

title: Weaver: Unlocking Blockchain Transaction Parallelism through State-Decoupled Symbolic Execution
text: Title: Weaver: Unlocking Blockchain Transaction Parallelism through State-Decoupled Symbolic Execution Ru Cheng , Maofan Yin , Liangrong Chen , Lizan Zhou , Chenyuan Wu Comments: 15 pages, 9 figures, 1 table Subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC) Transaction execution remains a major performance bottleneck in blockchains. Existing parallel execution engines are still blocked by slow state accesses on each transaction's critical path, creating a hidden loss of parallelism. This paper presents Weaver, a state-decoupled transaction processing paradigm that enables execution flow to proceed in the absence of concrete state values. Weaver represents states as lightweight symbolic references and records subsequent computation as symbolic expressions while concrete values are fetched on the fly. To handle state-dependent control flow, Weaver predicts the most likely branch direction through hierarchical symbolic pattern matching. Weaver further introduces expression-granular scheduling that evaluates each symbolic expression as soon as its state dependencies are resolved, rather than waiting for the transaction's entire read set, fully exploiting fine-grained intra-transaction parallelism. Evaluation on real Ethereum blocks and synthetic workloads spanning four representative dApps shows that Weaver delivers 41%-63% higher throughput than state-of-the-art parallel execution engines and up to 7.5 times the throughput of serial execution.

title: A 3D foundation model unifying CT interpretation and segmentation
text: Title: A 3D foundation model unifying CT interpretation and segmentation Yulu Xie , Zilong Li , Shen Xu , Yifan Bai , Liuhong Shi , Jiao Chen , Xianglei Kong , Wenchao Zhu , Na Shen , Xianghua Ye , Yang Yan , Jiaju Zheng , Yunsong Peng , Yanzhou Su , Chaohui Yu , Hao Luo , Fan Wang Comments: 114 pages, including Supplementary Information; 7 main figures and 2 Extended Data figures Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) Radiologists interpret computed tomography (CT) scans by jointly determining what a finding represents and where it lies in three-dimensional (3D) anatomy. However, CT models have treated CT interpretation and 3D segmentation as separate tasks, leaving textual findings spatially unverifiable and overlooking potential synergy between clinical understanding and spatial perception.
